questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining why meiosis halves the chromosome number and generates variation while mitosis keeps it constant, by comparing synapsis, crossing over and the separation of homologues and chromatids
questions.question: A student compares mitosis in onion root tip cells with meiosis in anther cells. Which explanation of the key mechanistic differences is correct?
options: A) In mitosis each chromosome's sister chromatids separate at anaphase, giving two daughter cells genetically identical to the parent with the same chromosome number; in meiosis I homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis, forming bivalents at zygotene), exchange segments by crossing over at pachytene (recombinase enzyme, chiasmata visible at diplotene), and the homologues — not the chromatids — separate at anaphase I, halving the chromosome number; meiosis II then separates sister chromatids, like mitosis, giving four haploid cells; the reduction division conserves the chromosome number across generations in sexually reproducing organisms, and crossing over plus independent assortment of bivalents increase genetic variability
B) Meiosis is a single division producing two diploid cells; crossing over occurs during mitotic prophase
C) In anaphase I sister chromatids separate, so meiosis I is equational
D) Mitosis halves the chromosome number; meiosis keeps it constant and produces identical cells
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Mitosis separates sister chromatids (equational); meiosis I separates homologues after synapsis and crossing over (reductional); meiosis II is equational.
Concept: Mitosis is the most dramatic period of the cell cycle; since the number of chromosomes in the parent and progeny cells is the same, it is also called equational division. In anaphase of mitosis, each chromosome arranged at the metaphase plate is split simultaneously and the two daughter chromatids, now referred to as chromosomes of the future daughter nuclei, begin their migration towards the two opposite poles. Mitosis usually results in the production of diploid daughter cells with identical genetic complement. The production of offspring by sexual reproduction includes the fusion of two gametes, each with a complete haploid set of chromosomes; gametes are formed from specialised diploid cells, and this specialised kind of cell division that reduces the chromosome number by half results in the production of haploid daughter cells; this kind of division is called meiosis. Meiosis involves two sequential cycles of nuclear and cell division called meiosis I and meiosis II but only a single cycle of DNA replication; meiosis I is initiated after the parental chromosomes have replicated to produce identical sister chromatids at the S phase. Meiosis involves pairing of homologous chromosomes and recombination between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes; four haploid cells are formed at the end of meiosis II. During zygotene of prophase I chromosomes start pairing together, a process called synapsis, accompanied by the formation of the synaptonemal complex; the complex formed by a pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes is called a bivalent or a tetrad. Pachytene is characterised by the appearance of recombination nodules, the sites at which crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of the homologous chromosomes; crossing over is the exchange of genetic material between two homologous chromosomes and is an enzyme-mediated process, the enzyme involved being called recombinase. In diplotene the X-shaped chiasmata become visible. In anaphase I, the homologous chromosomes separate, while sister chromatids remain associated at their centromeres. Meiosis II resembles a normal mitosis; at anaphase II the centromere of each chromosome splits, allowing the sister chromatids to move toward opposite poles. Meiosis is the mechanism by which conservation of specific chromosome number of each species is achieved across generations in sexually reproducing organisms, even though the process, per se, paradoxically, results in reduction of chromosome number by half; it also increases the genetic variability in the population of organisms from one generation to the next.
Why: Separating homologues rather than chromatids is what halves the number, and pairing with exchange is what creates new combinations.
Why not the others: (B) Meiosis has two divisions producing four haploid cells; crossing over is in meiotic prophase I. (C) Homologues separate in anaphase I, so meiosis I is reductional. (D) The roles are reversed.
Key point: Mitosis: chromatids separate (2n → 2n); meiosis I: homologues separate (2n → n); meiosis II: chromatids separate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Ordering the steps from light absorption by accessory pigments to the reaction centre and locating light and dark reactions in grana and stroma, using a chromatogram of leaf pigments
questions.question: A paper chromatogram of a leaf extract shows four bands. Which statement correctly identifies the pigments and the sequence of events in the chloroplast?
options: A) Chlorophyll b is the chief pigment and alone absorbs light; the dark reaction occurs in the grana and the light reaction in the stroma
B) Carotenoids directly fix CO₂; the thylakoid lumen is the site of the Calvin cycle

C) The bands are chlorophyll a (bright or blue-green), chlorophyll b (yellow-green), xanthophylls (yellow) and carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange); chlorophyll a is the chief pigment, and its absorption peaks in the blue and red regions coincide with the peaks of the action spectrum; the sequence is: accessory pigments (chlorophyll b, xanthophylls, carotenoids) absorb a wider range of wavelengths and pass the energy to chlorophyll a at the reaction centre of a light harvesting complex, which also protects chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation; the light reactions — absorption, water splitting, oxygen release and formation of ATP and NADPH — occur in the grana (thylakoid membranes), and the products are then used in the stroma, where enzymatic reactions synthesise sugar
D) The four bands are all forms of chlorophyll a differing only in concentration
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Chlorophyll a, b, xanthophylls and carotenoids; accessory pigments → chlorophyll a reaction centre → light reactions in grana → sugar synthesis in stroma.
Concept: Looking at plants have you ever wondered why and how there are so many shades of green in their leaves — even in the same plant? A chromatographic separation of the leaf pigments shows that the colour that we see in leaves is not due to a single pigment but due to four pigments: chlorophyll a (bright or blue green in the chromatograph), chlorophyll b (yellow green), xanthophylls (yellow) and carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange). Pigments are substances that have an ability to absorb light at specific wavelengths; chlorophyll a is the chief pigment associated with photosynthesis, and the wavelengths at which there is maximum absorption by chlorophyll a, i.e., in the blue and the red regions, also show a higher rate of photosynthesis. Though chlorophyll is the major pigment responsible for trapping light, other thylakoid pigments like chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids, which are called accessory pigments, also absorb light and transfer the energy to chlorophyll a; indeed, they not only enable a wider range of wavelength of incoming light to be utilised for photosynthesis but also protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation. The pigments are organised into two discrete photochemical light harvesting complexes (LHC) within Photosystem I and Photosystem II; each photosystem has all the pigments (except one molecule of chlorophyll a) forming a light harvesting system also called antennae, and the reaction centre is formed by a single chlorophyll a molecule. In the chloroplast, the membrane system is responsible for trapping the light energy and also for the synthesis of ATP and NADPH; in the stroma, enzymatic reactions synthesise sugar, which in turn forms starch. The former set of reactions, since they are directly light driven, are called light reactions (photochemical reactions); the latter are not directly light driven but are dependent on the products of light reactions (ATP and NADPH), hence to distinguish them they are called, by convention, dark reactions (carbon reactions).
Why: Energy flows from many antenna pigments to one reaction-centre chlorophyll a, and products of the membrane reactions feed the stromal reactions.
Why not the others: (A) Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment; light reactions are in grana and dark reactions in stroma. (B) Carotenoids are accessory pigments; the Calvin cycle runs in the stroma. (D) The bands are different pigments.
Key point: Accessory pigments → chlorophyll a (reaction centre); light reactions in grana, carbon reactions in stroma.

questions.sub_topic: Calculating respiratory quotients for carbohydrate, fat and organic acid substrates from balanced equations and interpreting RQ data, and explaining why respiration is called an amphibolic pathway
questions.question: Germinating seeds of three species gave these readings: seed X released 6 mL CO₂ for 6 mL O₂ used; seed Y released 102 mL CO₂ for 145 mL O₂; seed Z released 4 mL CO₂ for 3 mL O₂. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) All three respire only carbohydrate, since RQ is always 1

B) RQ of X = 1.0 (carbohydrate, e.g. C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O), Y ≈ 0.7 (fat, e.g. tripalmitin 2C₅₁H₉₈O₆ + 145O₂ → 102CO₂ + 98H₂O), Z ≈ 1.33 (organic acid such as malic acid); respiration is amphibolic because it is involved both in breakdown (catabolism) and synthesis (anabolism) — fats enter as glycerol (via PGAL) and fatty acids (via acetyl CoA), proteins as amino acids at various points in the Krebs cycle, and when fatty acids or other compounds are synthesised the same intermediates (e.g. acetyl CoA) are withdrawn from the pathway
C) RQ of Y is 1.42, showing protein; respiration is purely catabolic
D) RQ of Z is 0.75; Z is respiring fat
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) RQ: X = 1.0 (carbohydrate), Y ≈ 0.70 (fat), Z ≈ 1.33 (organic acid); respiration is amphibolic.
Concept: During aerobic respiration, O₂ is consumed and CO₂ is released; the ratio of the volume of CO₂ evolved to the volume of O₂ consumed in respiration is called the respiratory quotient (RQ) or respiratory ratio: RQ = volume of CO₂ evolved/volume of O₂ consumed. The respiratory quotient depends upon the type of respiratory substrate used during respiration. When carbohydrates are used as substrate and are completely oxidised, the RQ will be 1, because equal amounts of CO₂ and O₂ are evolved and consumed, respectively: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy, RQ = 6CO₂/6O₂ = 1.0. When fats are used in respiration the RQ is less than 1: for the fatty acid tripalmitin, 2(C₅₁H₉₈O₆) + 145O₂ → 102CO₂ + 98H₂O + energy, RQ = 102CO₂/145O₂ = 0.7. When proteins are respiratory substrates the ratio would be about 0.9. What is important to recognise is that in living organisms respiratory substrates are often more than one; pure proteins or fats are never used as respiratory substrates. Glucose is the favoured substrate for respiration, and all carbohydrates are usually first converted into glucose before they are used for respiration; other substrates can also be respired, but then they do not enter the respiratory pathway at the first step. Fats would need to be broken down into glycerol and fatty acids first; if fatty acids were to be respired they would first be degraded to acetyl CoA and enter the pathway; glycerol would enter the pathway after being converted to PGAL; the proteins would be degraded by proteases and the individual amino acids (after deamination), depending on their structure, would enter the pathway at some stage within the Krebs cycle or even as pyruvate or acetyl CoA. Since respiration involves breakdown of substrate, the respiratory process has traditionally been considered a catabolic process and the respiratory pathway a catabolic pathway; but when the organism needs to synthesise fatty acids, acetyl CoA would be withdrawn from the respiratory pathway for it; hence the respiratory pathway comes into the picture both during breakdown and synthesis of fatty acids, and similarly during breakdown and synthesis of protein too; because the respiratory pathway is involved in both anabolism and catabolism, it would hence be better to consider it as an amphibolic pathway rather than a catabolic one. Organic acids such as malic acid (C₄H₆O₅ + 3O₂ → 4CO₂ + 3H₂O) are oxygen-rich and give RQ greater than 1.
Given: X: 6/6; Y: 102/145; Z: 4/3.
Formula/Principle: RQ = volume CO₂ evolved/volume O₂ consumed.
Step 1: RQ(X) = 6/6 = 1.0 ⇒ carbohydrate.
Step 2: RQ(Y) = 102/145 = 0.70 ⇒ fat.
Step 3: RQ(Z) = 4/3 = 1.33 ⇒ organic acid (oxygen-rich substrate).
Why: Oxygen-poor substrates (fats) need more O₂ per CO₂, while oxygen-rich ones (organic acids) need less.
Why not the others: (A) RQ depends on substrate. (C) 102/145 ≈ 0.70, typical of fat; respiration is amphibolic. (D) 4/3 > 1, not a fat.
Key point: RQ: carbohydrate 1, fat ≈ 0.7, protein ≈ 0.9, organic acids > 1; respiration is amphibolic.

questions.sub_topic: Classifying the divisions of the peripheral nervous system and reading a table that assigns structures and effects to somatic, sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions and the visceral nervous system
questions.question: A table lists: (I) nerves carrying impulses from the CNS to skeletal muscles; (II) nerves carrying impulses from the CNS to involuntary organs and smooth muscles; (III) a division that, together with the other autonomic division, regulates internal organs; (IV) the complex of nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses by which impulses travel from the CNS to the viscera and back; (V) afferent fibres carrying impulses from tissues to the CNS. Which classification is correct?
options: A) (I) autonomic; (II) somatic; (III) part of CNS; (IV) brain stem; (V) efferent
B) All peripheral nerves are voluntary; the visceral nervous system is part of the CNS
C) (V) efferent; (I) sympathetic only

D) (I) somatic neural system; (II) autonomic neural system; (III) sympathetic or parasympathetic division (the autonomic system is further classified into these two); (IV) visceral nervous system, a part of the peripheral neural system; (V) afferent fibres — the PNS has afferent nerve fibres transmitting impulses from tissues/organs to the CNS and efferent fibres transmitting regulatory impulses from the CNS to the concerned peripheral tissues/organs; the PNS comprises all the nerves associated with the CNS (brain and spinal cord), and the CNS is the site of information processing and control
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) I somatic; II autonomic; III sympathetic/parasympathetic; IV visceral nervous system; V afferent.
Concept: The human neural system is divided into two parts: (i) the central neural system (CNS) and (ii) the peripheral neural system (PNS); the CNS includes the brain and the spinal cord and is the site of information processing and control; the PNS comprises all the nerves of the body associated with the CNS (brain and spinal cord). The nerve fibres of the PNS are of two types: (a) afferent fibres and (b) efferent fibres; the afferent nerve fibres transmit impulses from tissues/organs to the CNS and the efferent fibres transmit regulatory impulses from the CNS to the concerned peripheral tissues/organs. The PNS is divided into two divisions called the somatic neural system and the autonomic neural system; the somatic neural system relays impulses from the CNS to skeletal muscles, while the autonomic neural system transmits impulses from the CNS to the involuntary organs and smooth muscles of the body; the autonomic neural system is further classified into the sympathetic neural system and the parasympathetic neural system. The visceral nervous system is the part of the peripheral nervous system that comprises the whole complex of nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses by which impulses travel from the central nervous system to the viscera and from the viscera to the central nervous system.
Why: Divisions are defined by the target (skeletal muscle vs involuntary organs) and by the direction of the impulse (afferent vs efferent).
Why not the others: (A) Somatic and autonomic swapped; III and IV are peripheral; V is afferent. (B) Autonomic nerves are involuntary; the visceral system is peripheral. (C) V is afferent; I is somatic.
Key point: PNS → somatic (skeletal muscle) + autonomic (sympathetic, parasympathetic); visceral NS links CNS and viscera.

questions.sub_topic: Calculating recombination frequency and map distance from test-cross data for two linked genes, and relating Morgan's Drosophila results and Sturtevant's mapping to the chromosome theory
questions.question: In Drosophila, a dihybrid female heterozygous for two linked genes (parental arrangement AB/ab) is test-crossed with ab/ab. The progeny are: AB 450, ab 450, Ab 50, aB 50. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The genes assort independently, since all four classes appear
B) Recombination frequency = 50%; the genes are on different chromosomes

C) Recombination frequency = 100/1000 × 100 = 10%; the genes are 10 map units (centimorgans) apart; Morgan found that genes on the X chromosome did not segregate independently and that parental combinations were much more frequent than non-parental ones — for example, about 1.3% recombination between white eye and yellow body but 37.2% between white eye and miniature wing, so tightly linked genes show low recombination; Sturtevant used recombination frequency as a measure of distance between genes to map their positions on the chromosome, supporting the chromosome theory of inheritance proposed by Sutton and Boveri
D) Recombination frequency = 90%; the genes are very far apart
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) RF = 10%, map distance 10 cM; Morgan's linkage data and Sturtevant's mapping correctly described.
Concept: Sutton and Boveri argued that the pairing and separation of a pair of chromosomes would lead to the segregation of a pair of factors they carried; Sutton united the knowledge of chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles and called it the chromosomal theory of inheritance. Experimental verification of the chromosomal theory of inheritance by Thomas Hunt Morgan and his colleagues led to discovering the basis for the variation that sexual reproduction produced; Morgan worked with tiny fruit flies, Drosophila melanogaster, which were found very suitable for such studies — they could be grown on simple synthetic medium in the laboratory, complete their life cycle in about two weeks, a single mating could produce a large number of progeny flies, there was a clear differentiation of the sexes, and they have many types of hereditary variations that can be seen with low power microscopes. Morgan carried out several dihybrid crosses in Drosophila to study genes that were sex-linked; the crosses were similar to the dihybrid crosses carried out by Mendel in peas — for example, Morgan hybridised yellow-bodied, white-eyed females to brown-bodied, red-eyed males and intercrossed their F1 progeny; he observed that the two genes did not segregate independently of each other and the F2 ratio deviated very significantly from the 9:3:3:1 ratio. Morgan and his group knew that the genes were located on the X chromosome and saw quickly that when the two genes in a dihybrid cross were situated on the same chromosome, the proportion of parental gene combinations was much higher than the non-parental type; Morgan attributed this to the physical association or linkage of the two genes and coined the term linkage to describe this physical association of genes on a chromosome and the term recombination to describe the generation of non-parental gene combinations. Morgan and his group also found that even when genes were grouped on the same chromosome, some genes were very tightly linked (showed very low recombination) while others were loosely linked (showed higher recombination); for example, he found that the genes white and yellow were very tightly linked and showed only 1.3 per cent recombination while white and miniature wing showed 37.2 per cent recombination. His student Alfred Sturtevant used the frequency of recombination between gene pairs on the same chromosome as a measure of the distance between genes and 'mapped' their position on the chromosome.
Given: Parental 450 + 450 = 900; recombinant 50 + 50 = 100; total 1000.
Formula/Principle: RF (%) = recombinants/total × 100; 1% RF = 1 map unit (cM).
Step 1: Recombinants = 100.
Step 2: RF = 100/1000 × 100 = 10%.
Step 3: Map distance = 10 cM.
Why: Recombinants arise only by crossing over between the two loci, which is more likely the farther apart they are.
Why not the others: (A) Independent assortment gives a 1:1:1:1 ratio, not 9:9:1:1. (B) 50% is the maximum for unlinked genes; here only 10%. (D) 90% are parental, not recombinant.
Key point: RF = recombinants/total; low RF ⇒ tight linkage; RF used as map distance.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing XX–XY sex determination in humans, ZW–ZZ in birds and haplodiploidy in honey bees, and deciding which parent determines the sex of offspring in each
questions.question: Which comparison of sex-determining mechanisms is correct?
options: A) In humans males are heterogametic (XY, producing X- and Y-bearing sperm in equal proportion), so the sperm decides the sex of the child and each pregnancy has a 50% chance of a boy; in birds females are heterogametic (ZW) and males homogametic (ZZ), so the egg decides the sex of the chick; in honey bees an offspring formed from fertilised egg (diploid, 32 chromosomes) develops as a female (queen or worker) and one from an unfertilised egg develops as a male (drone, haploid, 16 chromosomes) by parthenogenesis — the haplodiploid system — so males produce sperm by mitosis and have no father (and thus cannot have sons) but have a grandfather and can have grandsons
B) In humans the mother's egg determines the sex because she has two X chromosomes
C) In birds males are heterogametic ZW; in honey bees males are diploid
D) Drones produce sperm by meiosis and have both a father and a mother
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Humans XX–XY (male heterogamety); birds ZW–ZZ (female heterogamety); honey bees haplodiploid.
Concept: Henking in 1891 could trace a specific nuclear structure all through spermatogenesis in a few insects, and it was also observed by him that 50 per cent of the sperm received this structure after spermatogenesis, whereas the other 50 per cent sperm did not receive it; he named it the X body, which was later named the X-chromosome. In a number of insects including grasshopper, the mechanism of sex determination is of the XO type, i.e., all eggs bear an additional X-chromosome besides the other chromosomes (autosomes), while some of the sperms bear the X-chromosome and some do not; eggs fertilised by sperm having an X-chromosome become females and those fertilised by sperms that do not have an X-chromosome become males. In a number of other insects and mammals including man, the XY type of sex determination is seen, where both male and female have the same number of chromosomes; among the males an X-chromosome is present but its counterpart is distinctly smaller and called the Y-chromosome; females, however, have a pair of X-chromosomes. In both cases (XO and XY) males produce two different types of gametes (either with or without X-chromosome, or some gametes with X-chromosome and some with Y-chromosome); such types of sex determination mechanism are designated to be examples of male heterogamety. In some other organisms, e.g., birds, a different mechanism of sex determination is observed: here the total number of chromosomes is the same in both males and females, but two different types of gametes in terms of the sex chromosomes are produced by females, i.e., female heterogamety; in order to have a distinction with the mechanism of sex determination described earlier, the two different sex chromosomes of a female bird have been designated to be the Z and W chromosomes; in these organisms the females have one Z and one W chromosome, whereas males have a pair of Z-chromosomes besides the autosomes. In humans, it is evident that it is the genetic makeup of the sperm that determines the sex of the child; it is also evident that in each pregnancy there is always a 50 per cent probability of either a male or a female child. Sex determination in honey bee is based on the number of sets of chromosomes an individual receives: an offspring formed from the union of a sperm and an egg develops as a female (queen or worker), and an unfertilised egg develops as a male (drone) by means of parthenogenesis; this means that the males have half the number of chromosomes than that of a female; the females are diploid having 32 chromosomes and males are haploid, i.e., having 16 chromosomes; this is called the haplodiploid sex-determination system and has special characteristic features such as the males produce sperms by mitosis, they do not have a father and thus cannot have sons, but have a grandfather and can have grandsons.
Why: The heterogametic parent supplies two kinds of gametes, so it decides the sex; in bees ploidy decides it.
Why not the others: (B) The father's sperm decides sex in humans. (C) Female birds are ZW; drones are haploid. (D) Drones make sperm by mitosis and have no father.
Key point: Humans: male heterogamety; birds: female heterogamety; bees: haplodiploidy.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the effects of a base substitution and a frameshift insertion or deletion on a reading frame, using the features of the genetic code and the sickle-cell example
questions.question: Using the sentence analogy RAM HAS RED CAP for a reading frame, compare (i) changing one letter, (ii) inserting one letter and (iii) inserting three letters. Which statement about the genetic code and mutations is correct?
options: A) Inserting one base changes only one amino acid, while a substitution shifts the whole reading frame
B) The code has 64 codons, all of which code for amino acids; there are no stop codons
C) Inserting three bases always destroys the entire protein from that point onward

D) A substitution of one base changes only one codon (RAM HAS BED CAP), as in sickle-cell anaemia where GAG → GUG replaces glutamic acid by valine at the sixth position of the β-globin chain; inserting or deleting one or two bases shifts the reading frame from that point (frameshift mutation), while inserting or deleting three bases adds or removes one amino acid and leaves the rest of the frame intact; the code is a triplet, 61 codons code for amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop codons, AUG codes for methionine and is the initiator codon, the code is unambiguous and specific, degenerate (some amino acids have more than one codon), read without punctuation, and nearly universal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Substitution changes one codon; 1–2 base insertions/deletions cause frameshifts; 3 bases change one amino acid; features of the code correct.
Concept: George Gamow argued that since there are only 4 bases and if they have to code for 20 amino acids, the code should constitute a combination of bases; he suggested that in order to code for all the 20 amino acids, the code should be made up of three nucleotides; this was a very bold proposition, because a permutation combination of 4³ (4 × 4 × 4) would generate 64 codons, generating many more codons than required. The salient features of the genetic code are as follows: (i) the codon is triplet — 61 codons code for amino acids and 3 codons do not code for any amino acids, hence they function as stop codons; (ii) some amino acids are coded by more than one codon, hence the code is degenerate; (iii) the codon is read in mRNA in a contiguous fashion — there are no punctuations; (iv) the code is nearly universal — for example, from bacteria to human UUU would code for phenylalanine (phe), with some exceptions in mitochondrial codons and in some protozoans; (v) one codon codes for only one amino acid, hence it is unambiguous and specific; (vi) AUG has dual functions — it codes for methionine (met), and it also acts as the initiator codon. The relationship between genes and DNA is best understood by mutation studies; effects of large deletions and rearrangements in a segment of DNA are easy to comprehend, as it may result in loss or gain of a gene and so a function. The effect of point mutations will be explained here; a classical example of point mutation is a change of a single base pair in the gene for beta globin chain that results in the change of amino acid residue glutamate to valine, resulting in a diseased condition called sickle cell anaemia. Effect of point mutations that inserts or deletes a base in the structural gene can be better understood by the following simple example: consider a statement RAM HAS RED CAP; if we insert a letter B in between HAS and RED and rearrange the statement, it would read RAM HAS BRE DCA P; similarly, if we now insert two letters at the same place, say BI, it would read RAM HAS BIR EDC AP; now we insert three letters together, say BIG, the statement would read RAM HAS BIG RED CAP; the same exercise can be repeated by deleting the letters R, E and D one by one and rearranging the statement to make a triplet word: RAM HAS EDC AP, RAM HAS DCA P, RAM HAS CAP. The conclusion from the above exercise is very obvious: insertion or deletion of one or two bases changes the reading frame from the point of insertion or deletion, while insertion or deletion of three or its multiple bases inserts or deletes one or multiple codons, hence one or multiple amino acids, and the reading frame remains unaltered from that point onwards; such mutations are referred to as frameshift insertion or deletion mutations.
Why: The code is read in fixed triplets without punctuation, so the effect depends on whether the change keeps the triplet frame.
Why not the others: (A) Effects reversed. (B) 3 of the 64 codons are stop codons. (C) Three-base insertions keep the frame.
Key point: Substitution → one codon changed; ±1 or ±2 bases → frameshift; ±3 → one amino acid added or lost.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting the length of a polypeptide translated from a short mRNA with start and stop codons, and the effect of a mutation that creates a premature stop codon, with the roles of tRNA and ribosome
questions.question: An mRNA has the sequence 5'-GCC AUG UUU GGC UAC AAA CCG UGA CUU-3'. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide translated from it? If a mutation changes the C of UAC to G, how many amino acids will the polypeptide have? Which statement about translation is correct?
options: A) 9 amino acids; 9 after mutation; translation starts from the first base and reads to the end

B) 6 amino acids (Met-Phe-Gly-Tyr-Lys-Pro); 3 after mutation, since UAC → UAG is a stop codon (nonsense mutation); translation begins at AUG, amino acids are first activated and linked to their cognate tRNAs (charging or aminoacylation, using ATP), tRNA acts as an adapter whose anticodon pairs with the codon, the ribosome's large subunit has two sites for tRNAs and its rRNA acts as a ribozyme forming peptide bonds; the bases before AUG and after UGA form untranslated regions (UTRs) needed for efficient translation, and a release factor binds the stop codon to end translation
C) 7 amino acids including one for UGA; 4 after mutation
D) 6 amino acids; 6 after mutation, because the code is degenerate
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 6 amino acids; 3 after the UAC → UAG change; translation mechanism correctly described.
Concept: Translation refers to the process of polymerisation of amino acids to form a polypeptide; the order and sequence of amino acids are defined by the sequence of bases in the mRNA, and the amino acids are joined by a bond which is known as a peptide bond; formation of a peptide bond requires energy, therefore in the first phase itself amino acids are activated in the presence of ATP and linked to their cognate tRNA — a process commonly called charging of tRNA or aminoacylation of tRNA, to be more specific. If two such charged tRNAs are brought close enough, the formation of peptide bond between them would be favoured energetically; the presence of a catalyst would enhance the rate of peptide bond formation. The cellular factory responsible for synthesising proteins is the ribosome; the ribosome consists of structural RNAs and about 80 different proteins; in its inactive state, it exists as two subunits, a large subunit and a small subunit; when the small subunit encounters an mRNA, the process of translation of the mRNA to protein begins; there are two sites in the large subunit for subsequent amino acids to bind to and thus be close enough to each other for the formation of a peptide bond; the ribosome also acts as a catalyst (23S rRNA in bacteria is the enzyme — ribozyme) for the formation of peptide bond. A translational unit in mRNA is the sequence of RNA that is flanked by the start codon (AUG) and the stop codon and codes for a polypeptide; an mRNA also has some additional sequences that are not translated and are referred to as untranslated regions (UTR); the UTRs are present at both 5'-end (before start codon) and at 3'-end (after stop codon), and they are required for an efficient translation process. For initiation, the ribosome binds to the mRNA at the start codon (AUG) that is recognised only by the initiator tRNA; the ribosome proceeds to the elongation phase of protein synthesis; during this stage, complexes composed of an amino acid linked to tRNA sequentially bind to the appropriate codon in mRNA by forming complementary base pairs with the tRNA anticodon; the ribosome moves from codon to codon along the mRNA; amino acids are added one by one, translated into polypeptide sequences dictated by DNA and represented by mRNA; at the end, a release factor binds to the stop codon, terminating translation and releasing the complete polypeptide from the ribosome.
Given: Reading frame from AUG: AUG UUU GGC UAC AAA CCG UGA.
Formula/Principle: Amino acids = codons from AUG up to (not including) the stop codon.
Step 1: AUG (Met), UUU (Phe), GGC (Gly), UAC (Tyr), AAA (Lys), CCG (Pro), then UGA stop ⇒ 6 amino acids.
Step 2: UAC → UAG (stop) at codon 4.
Step 3: Only Met-Phe-Gly ⇒ 3 amino acids.
Why: Translation runs from the start codon and halts at the first in-frame stop codon.
Why not the others: (A) GCC is in the 5' UTR and UGA stops translation. (C) Stop codons code for no amino acid. (D) UAG is a stop codon, not a synonym of UAC.
Key point: Count codons from AUG to the stop; a new stop codon truncates the protein.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Identifying founder effect, gene flow, mutation and natural selection in applied cases and explaining how each changes allele frequencies in a population
questions.question: Match the cases: (I) a few individuals colonise an island and their descendants have allele frequencies very different from the mainland population; (II) pollen from a crop field regularly reaches a nearby wild population; (III) bacteria on an antibiotic-containing medium — a few resistant mutants survive and soon the whole population is resistant; (IV) a new allele appears by a change in DNA. Which matching is correct?
options: A) I natural selection; II mutation; III gene flow; IV founder effect
B) All four are examples of genetic drift

C) I founder effect (genetic drift — chance change in allele frequency, the original drifted population becoming the founders); II gene migration or gene flow — when migration of a section of population to another place and population occurs, gene frequencies change in the original as well as in the new population; III natural selection (directional) acting on pre-existing variation; IV mutation, which creates new alleles and variation; together with genetic recombination, these are the factors affecting Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
D) I mutation; II natural selection; III founder effect; IV gene flow
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) I founder effect (drift); II gene flow; III natural selection; IV mutation.
Concept: Five factors are known to affect Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium: gene migration or gene flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection. When migration of a section of population to another place and population occurs, gene frequencies change in the original as well as in the new population; new genes/alleles are added to the new population and these are lost from the old population; there would be a gene flow if this gene migration happens multiple times. If the same change occurs by chance, it is called genetic drift; sometimes the change in allele frequency is so different in the new sample of population that they become a different species, and the original drifted population becomes the founders and the effect is called the founder effect. Microbial experiments show that pre-existing advantageous mutations, when selected, will result in observation of new phenotypes; over a few generations, this would result in speciation. Natural selection is a process in which heritable variations enabling better survival are enabled to reproduce and leave a greater number of progeny; natural selection can lead to stabilisation (in which more individuals acquire mean character value), directional change (more individuals acquire value other than the mean character value) or disruption (more individuals acquire peripheral character value at both ends of the distribution curve). Similarly, excess use of herbicides, pesticides, etc., has only resulted in selection of resistant varieties in a much lesser time scale; this is also true for microbes against which we employ antibiotics or drugs against eukaryotic organisms/cells — hence, resistant organisms/cells are appearing in a time scale of months or years and not centuries. Mutations are random and directionless, and they create the raw material (variation) on which selection acts.
Why: Each case changes allele frequencies by a different cause — chance sampling, migration, differential survival or new DNA change.
Why not the others: (A) Matches scrambled. (B) Only I is drift. (D) Matches scrambled.
Key point: Founder effect = drift; migration = gene flow; resistance = selection; new allele = mutation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Using brain capacities and time scales of fossil hominids to compare stages of human evolution, and recognising adaptive radiation in Darwin's finches and Australian marsupials
questions.question: Using these approximate figures — Homo habilis brain 650–800 cc, Homo erectus about 900 cc (about 1.5 mya), Neanderthal man 1400 cc (1,00,000–40,000 years ago) — find the ratio of Neanderthal to the upper Homo habilis brain capacity. Which statement about human evolution and adaptive radiation is correct?
options: A) Ratio 1.0; Homo habilis ate meat and buried the dead; adaptive radiation means convergent evolution
B) Ratio 0.57; Neanderthals arose before Homo habilis; Australian marsupials evolved from many unrelated ancestors
C) Ratio 2.15; Homo erectus is the earliest hominid; Darwin's finches all eat seeds

D) Ratio 1400/800 = 1.75; Homo habilis probably did not eat meat, Homo erectus probably ate meat, and Neanderthals buried their dead; Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus existed about 15 mya, modern Homo sapiens arose in Africa and moved across continents, and agriculture began about 10,000 years ago; adaptive radiation is the evolution of different species in a geographical area starting from a point and radiating to other habitats, as in Darwin's finches (seed-eaters giving rise to insectivorous forms with altered beaks) and Australian marsupials evolving from an ancestral stock within one island continent
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Ratio 1.75; habits and time scale of hominids, and adaptive radiation examples correct.
Concept: About 15 mya, primates called Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus were existing; they were hairy and walked like gorillas and chimpanzees; Ramapithecus was more man-like while Dryopithecus was more ape-like. Few fossils of man-like bones have been discovered in Ethiopia and Tanzania; these revealed hominid features leading to the belief that about 3–4 mya, man-like primates walked in eastern Africa; they were probably not taller than 4 feet but walked up right. Two mya, Australopithecines probably lived in East African grasslands; evidence shows they hunted with stone weapons but essentially ate fruit. Some of the bones among the bones discovered were different; this creature was called the first human-like being the hominid and was called Homo habilis; the brain capacities were between 650–800cc, and they probably did not eat meat. Fossils discovered in Java in 1891 revealed the next stage, i.e., Homo erectus about 1.5 mya; Homo erectus had a large brain around 900cc and probably ate meat. The Neanderthal man with a brain size of 1400cc lived in near east and central Asian countries between 1,00,000–40,000 years back; they used hides to protect their body and buried their dead. Homo sapiens arose in Africa and moved across continents and developed into distinct races; during the ice age between 75,000–10,000 years ago modern Homo sapiens arose; pre-historic cave art developed about 18,000 years ago, and agriculture came around 10,000 years back and human settlements started. During his journey Darwin went to the Galapagos Islands; there he observed an amazing diversity of creatures, of particular interest being small black birds later called Darwin's finches; he realised that there were many varieties of finches in the same island; all the varieties, he conjectured, evolved on the island itself; from the original seed-eating features, many other forms with altered beaks arose, enabling them to become insectivorous and vegetarian finches; this process of evolution of different species in a given geographical area starting from a point and literally radiating to other areas of geography (habitats) is called adaptive radiation. Another example is Australian marsupials: a number of marsupials, each different from the other, evolved from an ancestral stock, but all within the Australian island continent; when more than one adaptive radiation appeared to have occurred in an isolated geographical area (representing different habitats), one can call this convergent evolution — placental mammals in Australia also exhibit adaptive radiation in evolving into varieties of such placental mammals each of which appears to be 'similar' to a corresponding marsupial.
Given: Neanderthal 1400 cc; Homo habilis up to 800 cc.
Formula/Principle: Ratio = 1400/800.
Step 1: 1400/800 = 1.75.
Step 2: Order: Homo habilis → Homo erectus (≈1.5 mya, 900 cc) → Neanderthal (1400 cc).
Step 3: Brain size rises steadily through the sequence.
Why: Increasing brain capacity and changing habits (meat-eating, burial) mark successive hominid stages, while radiation from a common ancestor fills diverse habitats.
Why not the others: (A) Ratio wrong; burial is Neanderthal; adaptive radiation diverges from one ancestor. (B) Ratio inverted; order wrong; marsupials share an ancestral stock. (C) Ratio wrong; Homo habilis came earlier; finches diversified diets.
Key point: Brain 650–800 → 900 → 1400 cc; adaptive radiation from a common ancestor.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining loss of contact inhibition in cancer cells, the difference between benign and malignant tumours, the causes of cancer, and how cancer is detected and treated
questions.question: A patient's biopsy shows cells that keep dividing even when crowded and have invaded nearby tissue. Which statement about cancer is correct?
options: A) Cancer cells show strong contact inhibition; benign tumours spread through blood to distant sites

B) Normal cells show contact inhibition, by which contact with other cells inhibits their uncontrolled growth; cancer cells have lost this property and divide to form masses called tumours; benign tumours remain confined to their original location and cause little damage, while malignant tumours are masses of proliferating neoplastic cells that grow rapidly, invade and damage surrounding tissue, and send cells through blood to distant sites where they start new tumours (metastasis); carcinogens include ionising radiations (X-rays, gamma rays), non-ionising radiations (UV), chemicals (tobacco smoke) and oncogenic viruses, and cellular oncogenes (proto-oncogenes) when activated can cause transformation; cancer is detected by biopsy and histopathology, blood and bone marrow tests, radiography, CT and MRI, and treated by surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy and immunotherapy with biological response modifiers such as α-interferon
C) All tumours are malignant; cancer is caused only by viruses and cannot be detected before death
D) Chemotherapy has no side effects; MRI uses ionising X-rays to detect cancer
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Loss of contact inhibition; benign vs malignant (metastasis); carcinogens and oncogenes; detection and treatment correctly described.
Concept: Cancer is one of the most dreaded diseases of human beings and is a major cause of death all over the globe; in our body, cell growth and differentiation is highly controlled and regulated, and in cancer cells there is breakdown of these regulatory mechanisms. Normal cells show a property called contact inhibition by virtue of which contact with other cells inhibits their uncontrolled growth; cancer cells appear to have lost this property; as a result of this, cancerous cells just continue to divide giving rise to masses of cells called tumours. Tumours are of two types: benign and malignant; benign tumours normally remain confined to their original location and do not spread to other parts of the body and cause little damage; the malignant tumours, on the other hand, are a mass of proliferating cells called neoplastic or tumour cells; these cells grow very rapidly, invading and damaging the surrounding normal tissues; as these cells actively divide and grow they also starve the normal cells by competing for vital nutrients; cells sloughed from such tumours reach distant sites through blood, and wherever they get lodged in the body they start a new tumour there; this property, called metastasis, is the most feared property of malignant tumours. Transformation of normal cells into cancerous neoplastic cells may be induced by physical, chemical or biological agents, called carcinogens; ionising radiations like X-rays and gamma rays and non-ionising radiations like UV cause DNA damage leading to neoplastic transformation; the chemical carcinogens present in tobacco smoke have been identified as a major cause of lung cancer; cancer-causing viruses called oncogenic viruses have genes called viral oncogenes; furthermore, several genes called cellular oncogenes (c-onc) or proto-oncogenes have been identified in normal cells which, when activated under certain conditions, could lead to oncogenic transformation of the cells. Early detection of cancers is essential as it allows the disease to be treated successfully in many cases; cancer detection is based on biopsy and histopathological studies of the tissue and blood and bone marrow tests for increased cell counts in the case of leukemias; techniques like radiography (use of X-rays), CT (computed tomography) and MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) are very useful to detect cancers of the internal organs; MRI uses strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiations to accurately detect pathological and physiological changes in the living tissue. The common approaches for treatment of cancer are surgery, radiation therapy and immunotherapy; in radiotherapy, tumour cells are irradiated lethally, taking proper care of the normal tissues surrounding the tumour mass; several chemotherapeutic drugs are used to kill cancerous cells, and the majority of drugs have side effects like hair loss, anemia, etc.; most cancers are treated by a combination of surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy; tumour cells have been shown to avoid detection and destruction by the immune system, therefore the patients are given substances called biological response modifiers such as α-interferon which activates their immune system and helps in destroying the tumour.
Why: Losing growth control and contact inhibition lets cells multiply without limit, and the ability to invade and spread defines malignancy.
Why not the others: (A) Cancer cells lose contact inhibition; malignant, not benign, tumours metastasise. (C) Benign tumours exist; causes are varied; early detection is possible. (D) Chemotherapy has side effects; MRI uses magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation.
Key point: Loss of contact inhibition → tumour; malignant = invasion + metastasis; carcinogens, oncogenes; biopsy, CT, MRI; surgery, radiation, chemo, α-interferon.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the number of DNA copies produced after a given number of PCR cycles and describing denaturation, primer annealing and extension by a thermostable DNA polymerase
questions.question: A PCR starts with 10 copies of a target DNA. Assuming perfect doubling, how many copies are present after 20 cycles, and roughly how many does one molecule give after 30 cycles? Which description of the PCR steps is correct?
options: A) About 1.05 × 10⁷ copies (10 × 2²⁰); about 10⁹ copies (2³⁰ ≈ 1.07 × 10⁹); each cycle has denaturation of double-stranded DNA by high temperature, annealing of two sets of primers (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to regions of DNA), and extension by a thermostable DNA polymerase isolated from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus, which remains active during the high-temperature denaturation
B) 200 copies; 60 copies; primers are proteins; a heat-labile polymerase from E. coli is used
C) 10 × 20 = 200 copies; 2 × 30 = 60 copies; extension occurs before annealing
D) 2²⁰ = 10⁶ copies regardless of the starting amount; PCR uses RNA polymerase
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ≈ 1.05 × 10⁷ copies; ≈ 1 billion from one molecule after 30 cycles; denaturation, annealing, extension with Taq polymerase.
Concept: PCR stands for Polymerase Chain Reaction; in this reaction, multiple copies of the gene (or DNA) of interest are synthesised in vitro using two sets of primers (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides that are complementary to the regions of DNA) and the enzyme DNA polymerase; the enzyme extends the primers using the nucleotides provided in the reaction and the genomic DNA as template. If the process of replication of DNA is repeated many times, the segment of DNA can be amplified to approximately a billion times, i.e., 1 billion copies are made; such repeated amplification is achieved by the use of a thermostable DNA polymerase (isolated from a bacterium, Thermus aquaticus), which remains active during the high temperature induced denaturation of double-stranded DNA. The amplified fragment, if desired, can now be used to ligate with a vector for further cloning. Each cycle consists of three steps: denaturation, annealing and extension; since each cycle doubles the number of target molecules, the number after n cycles is N₀ × 2ⁿ.
Given: N₀ = 10; n = 20; and N₀ = 1, n = 30.
Formula/Principle: N = N₀ × 2ⁿ.
Step 1: 2²⁰ = 1 048 576 ≈ 1.05 × 10⁶.
Step 2: N = 10 × 1.05 × 10⁶ = 1.05 × 10⁷ copies.
Step 3: 2³⁰ = 1 073 741 824 ≈ 1.07 × 10⁹ (about a billion).
Why: Every cycle copies every existing strand, so the amount grows geometrically.
Why not the others: (B) Growth is exponential; primers are DNA oligonucleotides and a heat-stable polymerase is needed. (C) Multiplication instead of powers; the order of steps is wrong. (D) The starting amount multiplies the result; PCR uses DNA polymerase.
Key point: N = N₀ × 2ⁿ; denature → anneal primers → extend (Taq polymerase).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Using figures on rice and basmati diversity to discuss biopiracy and patents, and the roles of GEAC in biosafety and the Indian Patents Bill amendment
questions.question: India has an estimated 2,00,000 varieties of rice, of which 27 documented varieties are basmati. In 1997 an American company got patent rights on basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office. What percentage of India's rice varieties is basmati, and which statement about biopiracy, patents and biosafety is correct?
options: A) 27%; patents can be granted only on synthetic chemicals; GEAC is an international body that sells GM seeds
B) 2.7%; the basmati patent was granted to the Government of India; biopiracy is the legal sharing of benefits
C) 0.27%; biopiracy means only the theft of animals; GEAC has no role in GM research

D) 27/2,00,000 × 100 = 0.0135%; the patented 'new variety' was derived from Indian farmers' varieties crossed with semi-dwarf varieties, which could allow others selling basmati to be restricted; biopiracy is the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned and without compensatory payment; the Indian Parliament cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill to take such issues into consideration, and the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) makes decisions regarding the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.0135%; basmati patent, biopiracy, patents bill amendment and GEAC correctly described.
Concept: The modification/usage of living organisms for public services (as food and medicine sources, for example) has also created problems with patents granted for the same; there is growing public anger that certain companies are being granted patents for products and technologies that make use of the genetic materials, plants and other biological resources that have long been identified, developed and used by farmers and indigenous people of a specific region/country. Rice is an important food grain, the presence of which goes back thousands of years in Asia's agricultural history; there are an estimated 200,000 varieties of rice in India alone; the diversity of rice in India is one of the richest in the world, and Basmati rice is distinct for its unique aroma and flavour, with 27 documented varieties of Basmati grown in India; there is reference to Basmati in ancient texts, folklore and poetry, as it has been grown for centuries. In 1997, an American company got patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office; this allowed the company to sell a 'new' variety of Basmati, in the US and abroad; this 'new' variety of Basmati had actually been derived from Indian farmers' varieties — Indian Basmati was crossed with semi-dwarf varieties and claimed as an invention or a novelty; the patent extends to functional equivalents, implying that other people selling Basmati rice could be restricted by the patent. Several attempts have also been made to patent uses, products and processes based on Indian traditional herbal medicines, e.g., turmeric and neem. Biopiracy is the term used to refer to the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned without compensatory payment. Most of the industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge, while the developing and the underdeveloped world is rich in biodiversity and traditional knowledge related to bio-resources; there has to be a balance between them, and the Indian Parliament has recently cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill, that takes such issues into consideration, including patent terms, emergency provisions and research and development initiatives. The Indian Government has set up organisations such as GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee), which will make decisions regarding the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM-organisms for public services.
Given: 27 basmati varieties out of 2,00,000.
Formula/Principle: Percentage = part/whole × 100.
Step 1: 27/200 000 = 1.35 × 10⁻⁴.
Step 2: × 100 = 0.0135%.
Step 3: Basmati is a tiny but valuable fraction, which is why its patenting mattered.
Why: Patents on varieties derived from traditional ones without consent or payment constitute biopiracy.
Why not the others: (A) Percentage wrong; GEAC is an Indian regulatory body. (B) The patent went to an American company; biopiracy is unauthorised use. (C) Percentage wrong by a factor of 20; biopiracy covers bio-resources broadly; GEAC regulates GM research.
Key point: 27 of 2,00,000 rice varieties are basmati; biopiracy = unauthorised use without compensation; GEAC regulates GMOs.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting field observations on predator removal, biological control and parasite life cycles to explain the ecological roles of predation and parasitism
questions.question: Consider the observations: (I) prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia spread rapidly until a cactus-feeding predator (moth) from its natural habitat was introduced; (II) when the starfish Pisaster was removed from an intertidal community in America, more than 10 species of invertebrates became extinct within a year; (III) the human liver fluke needs two intermediate hosts (a snail and a fish); (IV) the cuckoo lays its eggs in the nest of the crow. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) I shows parasitism; II shows that predators reduce species diversity; III and IV are mutualism
B) Removing a predator always increases the number of prey species

C) I shows that predators keep prey populations under control, as used in biological control; II shows that predators help maintain species diversity by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species; III shows that parasites have complex life cycles with intermediate hosts to facilitate parasitisation of the primary host, and parasites may lose unnecessary sense organs, have adhesive organs or suckers, lose digestive systems and have high reproductive capacity; IV is brood parasitism, in which the parasitic bird's eggs resemble the host's eggs in size and colour to reduce the chance of detection; plants defend against herbivores by thorns (Acacia, cactus) and chemicals (Calotropis produces cardiac glycosides), while monarch butterflies become distasteful by acquiring chemicals from a poisonous weed eaten as caterpillars
D) III shows commensalism because the fluke benefits only the snail
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Biological control, predator-maintained diversity, complex parasite life cycles and brood parasitism correctly interpreted.
Concept: Predation is nature's way of transferring to higher trophic levels the energy fixed by plants; besides acting as 'conduits' for energy transfer across trophic levels, predators play other important roles — they keep prey populations under control; but for predators, prey species could achieve very high population densities and cause ecosystem instability. When certain exotic species are introduced into a geographical area, they become invasive and start spreading fast because the invaded land does not have its natural predators; the prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia in the early 1920s caused havoc by spreading rapidly into millions of hectares of rangeland; finally, the invasive cactus was brought under control only after a cactus-feeding predator (a moth) from its natural habitat was introduced into the country; biological control methods adopted in agricultural pest control are based on the ability of the predator to regulate prey population. Predators also help in maintaining species diversity in a community, by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species; in the rocky intertidal communities of the American Pacific Coast the starfish Pisaster is an important predator; in a field experiment, when all the starfish were removed from an enclosed intertidal area, more than 10 species of invertebrates became extinct within a year, because of interspecific competition. If a predator is too efficient and overexploits its prey, then the prey might become extinct and following it, the predator will also become extinct for lack of food. Prey species have evolved various defences to lessen the impact of predation: some species of insects and frogs are cryptically-coloured (camouflaged) to avoid being detected easily by the predator; some are poisonous and therefore avoided by the predators — the monarch butterfly is highly distasteful to its predator (bird) because of a special chemical present in its body, which it acquires during its caterpillar stage by feeding on a poisonous weed. For plants, herbivores are the predators; nearly 25 per cent of all insects are known to be phytophagous; the most common morphological means of defence are the thorns (Acacia, cactus); many plants produce and store chemicals that make the herbivore sick when they are eaten, inhibit feeding or digestion, disrupt its reproduction or even kill it — the weed Calotropis growing in abandoned fields produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides, and that is why you never see any cattle or goats browsing on this plant. Parasitism: many parasites have evolved to be host-specific in such a way that both host and the parasite tend to co-evolve; in accordance with their life styles, parasites evolved special adaptations such as the loss of unnecessary sense organs, presence of adhesive organs or suckers to cling on to the host, loss of digestive system and high reproductive capacity; the life cycles of parasites are often complex, involving one or two intermediate hosts or vectors to facilitate parasitisation of its primary host; the human liver fluke (a trematode parasite) depends on two intermediate hosts (a snail and a fish) to complete its life cycle. Brood parasitism in birds is a fascinating example of parasitism in which the parasitic bird lays its eggs in the nest of its host and lets the host incubate them; during the course of evolution, the eggs of the parasitic bird have evolved to resemble the host's egg in size and colour to reduce the chances of the host bird detecting the foreign eggs and ejecting them from the nest; try to follow the movements of the cuckoo (koel) and the crow in your neighbourhood park during the breeding season (spring to summer) and watch brood parasitism in action.
Why: Predators regulate prey and relieve competition, while parasites evolve specialised life cycles and deceptive strategies to exploit hosts.
Why not the others: (A) I is predation; predators maintain diversity; III and IV are parasitism. (B) Removing Pisaster reduced the number of species. (D) The fluke parasitises its hosts.
Key point: Predation controls prey and maintains diversity; parasites have complex life cycles; cuckoo shows brood parasitism.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Constructing pyramids of numbers, biomass and energy from field data, and explaining why the biomass pyramid in a sea can be inverted while the energy pyramid is always upright
questions.question: A student samples a sea ecosystem and finds standing crops (dry mass per m²): phytoplankton 4 g, zooplankton 21 g, small fish 10 g. A separate study of a single large tree records 1 tree supporting 3000 insects and 15 birds. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The sea's biomass pyramid is inverted because the small standing crop of fast-reproducing phytoplankton supports a larger biomass of consumers; the tree data give an inverted pyramid of numbers (one producer supporting many insects); however, the pyramid of energy is always upright, because energy at each trophic level is less than at the level below, some being lost as heat at each step; ecological pyramids assume simple food chains, do not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels, and saprophytes are not given any place in them
B) The sea data show an upright pyramid of biomass; the pyramid of energy can be inverted when producers are small
C) The tree data give an upright pyramid of numbers; energy increases at higher trophic levels
D) Pyramids of energy are inverted in the sea because fish have more biomass than phytoplankton
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Inverted biomass pyramid in sea; inverted pyramid of numbers for the tree; energy pyramid always upright.
Concept: The relationship between producers and consumers in an ecosystem can be graphically represented in the form of a pyramid called an ecological pyramid; the base of each pyramid represents the producers or the first trophic level while the apex represents the tertiary or top level consumer; the three ecological pyramids that are usually studied are (a) pyramid of number, (b) pyramid of biomass and (c) pyramid of energy. Each trophic level has a certain mass of living material at a particular time called the standing crop; the standing crop is measured as the biomass of living organisms (biomass) or the number in a unit area; the biomass of a species is expressed in terms of fresh or dry weight, and measurement of biomass in terms of dry weight is more accurate. In most ecosystems, all the pyramids — of number, of energy and biomass — are upright, i.e., producers are more in number and biomass than the herbivores, and herbivores are more in number and biomass than the carnivores; also energy at a lower trophic level is always more than at a higher level. There are exceptions to this generalisation: if you were to count the number of insects feeding on a big tree, what kind of pyramid would you get? and now add an estimate of the number of small birds depending on the insects, as also the number of larger birds eating the smaller — this would be an inverted pyramid of numbers. The pyramid of biomass in sea is also generally inverted because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton. A pyramid of energy is always upright and can never be inverted, because when energy flows from a particular trophic level to the next trophic level, some energy is always lost as heat at each step; each bar in the energy pyramid indicates the amount of energy present at each trophic level in a given time or annually per unit area. However, there are certain limitations of ecological pyramids such as: it does not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels; it assumes a simple food chain, something that almost never exists in nature, as it does not accommodate a food web; moreover, saprophytes are not given any place in ecological pyramids even though they play a vital role in the ecosystem.
Given: Sea: 4 → 21 → 10 g m⁻²; tree: 1 → 3000 → 15.
Formula/Principle: Pyramid shape follows the relative size of successive trophic levels; energy always decreases upward.
Step 1: Producer biomass (4) < primary consumer biomass (21) ⇒ inverted base of the biomass pyramid.
Step 2: 1 tree < 3000 insects ⇒ inverted (spindle-shaped) pyramid of numbers.
Step 3: Energy transferred is roughly 10% at each step ⇒ always upright.
Why: Standing crop is a snapshot that ignores turnover rate, while energy flow per unit time always decreases up the chain.
Why not the others: (B) The sea biomass pyramid is inverted; the energy pyramid cannot be inverted. (C) One tree supporting thousands of insects gives an inverted number pyramid; energy decreases upward. (D) The energy pyramid is never inverted.
Key point: Biomass (sea) and number (tree) pyramids can be inverted; energy pyramid always upright.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Sorting conservation measures into in situ and ex situ categories from a table, and recalling IUCN Red List extinction figures and the purpose of the Ramsar convention on wetlands
questions.question: A table lists: zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks, cryopreservation of gametes, seed banks, biosphere reserves, national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and sacred groves. Which classification and statement is correct?
options: A) All are in situ; the IUCN Red List (2004) records no extinctions in the last 500 years

B) Ex situ (off site): zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks, cryopreservation of gametes in viable and fertile condition, and seed banks; in situ (on site): biosphere reserves, national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and sacred groves; the IUCN Red List (2004) documents the extinction of 784 species (338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants) in the last 500 years, and the Ramsar Convention is an international treaty for the conservation and wise use of wetlands
C) Seed banks and sacred groves are in situ; zoos are in situ; the Ramsar Convention deals with deserts
D) Biosphere reserves are ex situ; cryopreservation is in situ
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ex situ: zoos, botanical gardens, safari parks, cryopreservation, seed banks; in situ: biosphere reserves, national parks, sanctuaries, sacred groves; Red List and Ramsar correctly described.
Concept: When we conserve and protect the whole ecosystem, its biodiversity at all levels is protected — we save the entire forest to save the tiger; this approach is called in situ (on site) conservation. However, when there is a situation where an animal or plant is endangered or threatened and needs urgent measures to save it from extinction, ex situ (off site) conservation is the desirable approach. In situ conservation: India now has 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks and 448 wildlife sanctuaries; India has also a history of religious and cultural traditions that emphasised protection of nature — in many cultures, tracts of forest were set aside, and all the trees and wildlife within were venerated and given total protection; such sacred groves are found in Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh. In ex situ conservation, threatened animals and plants are taken out from their natural habitat and placed in special settings where they can be protected and given special care; zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks serve this purpose; there are many animals that have become extinct in the wild but continue to be maintained in zoological parks. In recent years ex situ conservation has advanced beyond keeping threatened species; now gametes of threatened species can be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods using cryopreservation techniques, eggs can be fertilised in vitro, and plants can be propagated using tissue culture methods; seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be kept for long periods in seed banks. The colourful stories of evolution and extinction: the IUCN Red List (2004) documents the extinction of 784 species (including 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants) in the last 500 years; some examples of recent extinctions include the dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller's Sea Cow (Russia) and three subspecies (Bali, Javan, Caspian) of tiger. The Ramsar Convention (1971) is an intergovernmental treaty providing the framework for the conservation and wise use of wetlands and their resources.
Why: The deciding question is whether the organism is protected in its natural habitat or removed to a managed setting.
Why not the others: (A) Several are ex situ; 784 extinctions are recorded. (C) Seed banks and zoos are ex situ; Ramsar concerns wetlands. (D) Biosphere reserves are in situ; cryopreservation is ex situ.
Key point: In situ = protect habitat; ex situ = zoos, gardens, seed banks, cryopreservation; Red List 784 extinctions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Writing a scientific name correctly under binomial nomenclature and placing an organism in the taxonomic hierarchy, with the three-domain system as a higher category
questions.question: A student writes the name of mango and its classification. Which version is correct?
options: A) mangifera Indica; Kingdom → Species → Genus → Family; the three domains are Plantae, Animalia and Fungi
B) Mangifera Indica (both capitalised, not italicised); hierarchy Species → Order → Family → Class
C) Indica mangifera; classification from Phylum directly to Species

D) Mangifera indica (Linn.), with the genus name starting with a capital letter and the specific epithet with a small letter, printed in italics or, when handwritten, underlined separately; the hierarchy from lowest to highest is Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum (Division for plants) → Kingdom, with mango in family Anacardiaceae, order Sapindales, class Dicotyledonae and division Angiospermae; man is Homo sapiens in family Hominidae, order Primata, class Mammalia and phylum Chordata; above the kingdoms, the three-domain system (Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya) divides life on the basis of molecular differences
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Mangifera indica written correctly; correct hierarchy and placements; three domains Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya.
Concept: There are millions of plants and animals in the world; we know the plants and animals in our own area by their local names, which would vary from place to place even within a country; hence there is a need to standardise the naming of living organisms such that a particular organism is known by the same name all over the world, and this process is called nomenclature. Biologists follow universally accepted principles to provide scientific names to known organisms; each name has two components — the generic name and the specific epithet; this system of providing a name with two components is called binomial nomenclature, given by Carolus Linnaeus. Let us take the example of mango to understand the way of providing scientific names better: the scientific name of mango is written as Mangifera indica; in this name Mangifera represents the genus while indica is a particular species, or a specific epithet. Other universal rules of nomenclature are as follows: biological names are generally in Latin and written in italics; the first word in a biological name represents the genus while the second component denotes the specific epithet; both the words in a biological name, when handwritten, are separately underlined, or printed in italics to indicate their Latin origin; the first word denoting the genus starts with a capital letter while the specific epithet starts with a small letter; the name of the author appears after the specific epithet, i.e., at the end of the biological name and is written in an abbreviated form, e.g., Mangifera indica Linn., which indicates that this species was first described by Linnaeus. Classification is not a single step process but involves a hierarchy of steps in which each step represents a rank or category; since the category is a part of overall taxonomic arrangement, it is called the taxonomic category and all categories together constitute the taxonomic hierarchy. The taxonomic categories in ascending order are species, genus, family, order, class, phylum (division in plants) and kingdom; for example, man (Homo sapiens) belongs to family Hominidae, order Primata, class Mammalia, phylum Chordata, kingdom Animalia; mango (Mangifera indica) belongs to family Anacardiaceae, order Sapindales, class Dicotyledonae, division Angiospermae, kingdom Plantae. A three-domain system has also been proposed that divides the kingdom Monera into two domains, leaving the remaining eukaryotic kingdoms in the third domain and thereby a six-kingdom classification.
Why: Fixed rules for writing names and a nested hierarchy give every organism one universal name and a unique place.
Why not the others: (A) Capitalisation reversed; hierarchy wrong; those are kingdoms, not domains. (B) The epithet is lower-case and the name italicised; order of ranks wrong. (C) Genus comes first; intermediate ranks are skipped.
Key point: Genus (capital) + species (small), italic; species → genus → family → order → class → phylum → kingdom.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Distinguishing a dicot stem from a monocot stem in transverse section by hypodermis, arrangement and type of vascular bundles, bundle sheath, pith and phloem parenchyma
questions.question: Two transverse sections of stems are compared. Section P has a collenchymatous hypodermis, a starch-rich endodermis, vascular bundles arranged in a ring, each conjoint, collateral and open with endarch protoxylem, and a large pith. Section Q has a sclerenchymatous hypodermis, numerous scattered vascular bundles each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, closed bundles, water-containing cavities, no phloem parenchyma and no distinct pith. Which identification is correct?
options: A) P is a dicot stem and Q is a monocot stem; in the dicot stem the epidermis has a thin cuticle and may bear trichomes and a few stomata, the hypodermis is a few layers of collenchyma, the cortex inside it is parenchymatous, the innermost cortical layer (endodermis) is rich in starch grains (starch sheath), the pericycle is present as semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma, and the presence of cambium between xylem and phloem makes the bundles open and allows secondary growth; the monocot stem's closed bundles lack cambium, so secondary growth does not normally occur
B) P is a monocot stem and Q is a dicot stem
C) Both are roots because they have endodermis
D) Q is a dicot stem because its bundles are scattered and closed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) P = dicot stem (ring of open bundles, pith); Q = monocot stem (scattered closed bundles, sclerenchymatous hypodermis).
Concept: The transverse section of a typical young dicotyledonous stem shows that the epidermis is the outermost protective layer of the stem; covered with a thin layer of cuticle, it may bear trichomes and a few stomata. The cells arranged in multiple layers between the epidermis and pericycle constitute the cortex, which consists of three sub-zones: the outer hypodermis consists of a few layers of collenchymatous cells just below the epidermis, which provide mechanical strength to the young stem; cortical layers below the hypodermis consist of rounded thin-walled parenchymatous cells with conspicuous intercellular spaces; the innermost layer of the cortex is called the endodermis, and the cells of the endodermis are rich in starch grains and the layer is also referred to as the starch sheath. Pericycle is present on the inner side of the endodermis and above the phloem in the form of semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma; in between the vascular bundles there are a few layers of radially placed parenchymatous cells, which constitute medullary rays. A large number of vascular bundles are arranged in a ring; the 'ring' arrangement of vascular bundles is a characteristic of the dicot stem; each vascular bundle is conjoint, open, and with endarch protoxylem; a large number of rounded, parenchymatous cells with large intercellular spaces which occupy the central portion of the stem constitute the pith.
