The order of a reaction is sometimes altered by conditions: in the hydrolysis of ethyl acetate, CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O → CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH, the concentration of water does not get altered much during the course of the reaction, so the rate depends only on [ester] — such reactions are called pseudo first order reactions.
Given: Rate = k[A]¹[B]².
Formula/Principle: Order = sum of exponents; units of k = (mol L⁻¹)¹⁻ⁿ s⁻¹.
Step 1: n = 1 + 2 = 3.
Step 2: Rate factor = 2¹ × 2² = 8.
Step 3: Units: (mol L⁻¹)⁻² s⁻¹ = mol⁻² L² s⁻¹.
Why: The rate law, not the balanced equation, gives the order, and molecularity applies only to single elementary steps.
Why not the others: (A) Order is 3; molecularity need not match. (C) Doubling [B] quadruples the rate; s⁻¹ is for first order. (D) Molecularity is a whole number; order is experimental.
Key point: Order = Σ exponents; k units (mol L⁻¹)¹⁻ⁿ s⁻¹; molecularity is integral and only for elementary steps.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining trends in atomic radii and ionisation enthalpies across the 3d series and down groups of transition elements, including the effect of lanthanoid contraction on 4d and 5d radii
questions.question: Which statement about trends in the d-block is correct?
options: A) Atomic radii increase steadily across the 3d series; Zr and Hf differ greatly in radius
B) Ionisation enthalpies decrease steadily across each transition series

C) Across the 3d series atomic radii decrease at first and then become nearly constant, because each added 3d electron shields the outer electrons poorly but increasing interelectronic repulsion offsets the rising nuclear charge; ionisation enthalpies increase only gradually and irregularly across the series; 4d radii are larger than 3d, but 4d and 5d elements of a group have almost identical radii (Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm) because of lanthanoid contraction — the poor shielding by 4f electrons filled before the 5d series; Zn, Cd and Hg, with completely filled d orbitals, have low enthalpies of atomisation and relatively high first ionisation enthalpies
D) Lanthanoid contraction makes 5d elements much larger than 4d elements
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Radii decrease then level off; IE rises irregularly; lanthanoid contraction makes 4d and 5d radii similar.
Concept: In general, ions of the same charge in a given series show progressive decrease in radius with increasing atomic number; this is because the new electron enters a d orbital each time the nuclear charge increases by unity; it may be recalled that the shielding effect of a d electron is not that effective, hence the net electrostatic attraction between the nuclear charge and the outermost electron increases and the ionic radius decreases; the same trend is observed in the atomic radii of a given series; however, the variation within a series is quite small. An interesting point emerges when atomic sizes of one series are compared with those of the corresponding elements in the other series: the curves show an increase from the first (3d) to the second (4d) series of the elements, but the radii of the third (5d) series are virtually the same as those of the corresponding members of the second series; this phenomenon is associated with the intervention of the 4f orbitals which must be filled before the 5d series of elements begin; the filling of 4f before 5d orbital results in a regular decrease in atomic radii called lanthanoid contraction, which essentially compensates for the expected increase in atomic size with increasing atomic number; the net result of the lanthanoid contraction is that the second and the third d series exhibit similar radii (e.g., Zr 160 pm, Hf 159 pm) and have very similar physical and chemical properties much more than that expected on the basis of usual family relationship. Due to an increase in nuclear charge which accompanies the filling of the inner d orbitals, there is an increase in ionisation enthalpy along each series of the transition elements from left to right; however, many small variations occur; the irregular trend in the first ionisation enthalpy of the metals of the 3d series, though of little chemical significance, can be accounted for by considering that the removal of one electron alters the relative energies of 4s and 3d orbitals. The transition elements (with the exception of Zn, Cd and Hg) are very much hard and have low volatility; Zn, Cd and Hg have completely filled d orbitals and no unpaired electrons for metallic bonding, so their enthalpies of atomisation are low.
Why: Poorly shielding inner d and f electrons increase the effective nuclear charge felt by outer electrons.
Why not the others: (A) Radii decrease; Zr and Hf have nearly the same radius. (B) IE increases across the series. (D) Lanthanoid contraction offsets the expected increase.
Key point: 3d radii decrease then level; IE rises irregularly; lanthanoid contraction ⇒ 4d ≈ 5d radii.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Testing linear, square and modulus functions for one-one and onto behaviour on different domains and codomains using their graphs, and counting one-one functions between finite sets
questions.question: Which classification is correct for \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R,\ f(x)=2x+3\); \(g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R,\ g(x)=x^2\); \(h:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N,\ h(x)=x^2\); and how many one-one functions are there from a 3-element set to a 4-element set?
options: A) \(f\text{ bijective};\ g\text{ one-one};\ h\text{ onto};\ 64\)
B) \(f\text{ bijective (every horizontal line meets its graph exactly once)};\ g\text{ neither one-one nor onto};\ h\text{ one-one but not onto};\ ^4P_3=24\)
C) \(f\text{ one-one only};\ g\text{ onto};\ h\text{ bijective};\ 12\)
D) \(f\text{ bijective};\ g\text{ neither};\ h\text{ neither};\ 81\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(f\text{ bijective};\ g\text{ neither};\ h\text{ one-one, not onto};\ 24\)
Concept: \(\text{one-one: distinct inputs give distinct outputs (horizontal line meets graph at most once); onto: every element of the codomain is an image}\)
Given: \(f(x)=2x+3,\ g(x)=x^2,\ h(x)=x^2\ \text{on }\mathbb N\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{one-one: }f(a)=f(b)\Rightarrow a=b;\ \text{onto: range}=\text{codomain};\ \#\text{one-one}=\,^nP_m\)
Step 1: \(2a+3=2b+3\Rightarrow a=b;\ y=2x+3\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{y-3}{2}\in\mathbb R\Rightarrow f\text{ bijective}\)
Step 2: \(g(-1)=g(1)\Rightarrow\text{not one-one};\ g(x)\ne-1\Rightarrow\text{not onto}\)
Step 3: \(h\text{ one-one on }\mathbb N;\ 2\text{ is not a square}\Rightarrow\text{not onto};\ 4\times3\times2=24\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{one-one maps }\{a,b,c\}\to\{1,2,3,4\}:\ 4\cdot3\cdot2=\,^4P_3=24\]
Check: \[\text{total functions}=4^3=64>24\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{restricting the domain to }\mathbb N\text{ removes the negative inputs that spoil one-one-ness, but not all naturals are squares}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(g\text{ is not one-one; }h\text{ not onto; 64 counts all functions}\); (C) \(f\text{ is also onto}\); (D) \(h\text{ is one-one}\).
Key point: \(\text{horizontal line test};\ \#\text{one-one}=\,^nP_m\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using an additive functional equation to find function values, finding the size of a domain from the number of functions, and counting bijections of a finite set
questions.question: If \(f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\) for all real \(x,y\) and \(f(1)=3\), find \(f(5)\) and \(f(0)\). If there are 64 functions from a set \(A\) to a set \(B\) with \(n(B)=4\), find \(n(A)\). How many bijections does a 3-element set have onto itself?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(f(5)=15,\ f(0)=0;\ n(A)=3;\ 6\)
Concept: \(\text{the number of functions from an }m\text{-element set to an }n\text{-element set is }n^m;\ \text{the number of bijections of an }n\text{-element set is }n!\)
Given: \(f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y),\ f(1)=3;\ 64\text{ functions},\ n(B)=4\)
Formula/Principle: \(f(nx)=nf(x)\ (n\in\mathbb N);\ n(B)^{n(A)}\)
Step 1: \(x=y=0:\ f(0)=2f(0)\Rightarrow f(0)=0\)
Step 2: \(f(5)=f(1)+f(1)+f(1)+f(1)+f(1)=15\)
Step 3: \(4^{n(A)}=64\Rightarrow n(A)=3;\ 3!=6\)
Worked derivation: \[f(2)=f(1+1)=2f(1),\ \dots,\ f(n)=nf(1)\Rightarrow f(5)=5\times3\]
Check: \[4^3=64\ \checkmark;\quad f(0+0)=f(0)+f(0)=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{additivity forces }f\text{ to be linear on integers and to vanish at }0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{additivity gives }5f(1);\ 4^3=64\); (B) \(\text{used a multiplicative rule}\); (C) \(f(0)=0;\ n(A)=3;\ 3!=6\).
Key point: \(f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\Rightarrow f(0)=0,\ f(n)=nf(1);\ n^m\text{ functions}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Writing general solutions of sine, cosine and tangent equations, solving a quadratic in sine, and locating solutions as intersections of a horizontal line with the graph
questions.question: Find the general solution of \(2\cos^2x+3\sin x=0\). How many solutions does \(\sin x=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) have in \([0,2\pi]\), and what is the general solution of \(\tan x=\sqrt3\)?
options: A) \(x=n\pi+(-1)^{n}\tfrac{7\pi}{6}\ (\sin x=-\tfrac12);\ 2\ (x=\tfrac\pi3,\tfrac{2\pi}3,\ \text{where }y=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\text{ meets the sine curve});\ x=n\pi+\tfrac\pi3\)
B) \(x=n\pi+(-1)^n\tfrac\pi6;\ 1;\ x=2n\pi+\tfrac\pi3\)
C) \(x=2n\pi\pm\tfrac{2\pi}{3};\ 4;\ x=n\pi-\tfrac\pi3\)
D) \(\text{no solution};\ 2;\ x=n\pi+\tfrac\pi6\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(x=n\pi+(-1)^n\tfrac{7\pi}{6};\ 2\text{ solutions};\ x=n\pi+\tfrac\pi3\)
Concept: \(\sin x=\sin y\Rightarrow x=n\pi+(-1)^ny;\ \cos x=\cos y\Rightarrow x=2n\pi\pm y;\ \tan x=\tan y\Rightarrow x=n\pi+y\)
Given: \(2\cos^2x+3\sin x=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x\)
Step 1: \(2-2\sin^2x+3\sin x=0\Rightarrow2\sin^2x-3\sin x-2=0\Rightarrow(2\sin x+1)(\sin x-2)=0\)
Step 2: \(\sin x=2\text{ impossible};\ \sin x=-\tfrac12=\sin\tfrac{7\pi}{6}\Rightarrow x=n\pi+(-1)^n\tfrac{7\pi}6\)
Step 3: \(\sin x=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2:\ x=\tfrac\pi3,\tfrac{2\pi}3\ \text{in }[0,2\pi];\ \tan x=\tan\tfrac\pi3\Rightarrow x=n\pi+\tfrac\pi3\)
Worked derivation: \[2\sin^2x-3\sin x-2=(2\sin x+1)(\sin x-2)\]
Check: \[x=\tfrac{7\pi}6:\ 2\cdot\tfrac34+3\left(-\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac32-\tfrac32=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{converting to a quadratic in }\sin x\text{ and rejecting }|\sin x|>1\text{ leaves one family}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\sin x=-\tfrac12,\ \text{not }+\tfrac12;\ \text{tangent period is }\pi\); (C) \(\text{wrong root and count}\); (D) \(\text{a solution exists}\).
Key point: \(\text{reduce to one trig function; reject impossible roots}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting integer values of a coefficient for which a quadratic has integer roots, and finding all rational roots of a cubic using the rational root test and factor theorem
questions.question: For how many integer values of \(p\) does \(x^2+px+12=0\) have integer roots? Find all roots of \(2x^3-3x^2-3x+2=0\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(6\text{ values};\ \text{roots }2,-1,\tfrac12\)
Concept: \(\text{integer roots }\alpha,\beta\text{ satisfy }\alpha\beta=12,\ \alpha+\beta=-p;\ \text{a rational root }\tfrac pq\text{ of an integer polynomial has }p\mid a_0\text{ and }q\mid a_n\)
Given: \(\alpha\beta=12;\ 2x^3-3x^2-3x+2\)
Formula/Principle: \(p=-(\alpha+\beta);\ \text{candidates }\pm1,\pm2,\pm\tfrac12\)
Step 1: \(\{\alpha,\beta\}=\{1,12\},\{2,6\},\{3,4\}\text{ and negatives}\Rightarrow p=\mp13,\mp8,\mp7\Rightarrow6\)
Step 2: \(f(2)=16-12-6+2=0;\ f(-1)=-2-3+3+2=0\)
Step 3: \(\text{product of roots}=-\tfrac22=-1\Rightarrow2\cdot(-1)\cdot r=-1\Rightarrow r=\tfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[2x^3-3x^2-3x+2=(x-2)(x+1)(2x-1)\]
Check: \[f\!\left(\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac14-\tfrac34-\tfrac32+2=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{Vieta's relations limit integer roots to factor pairs, and the rational root test limits candidates}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{negative pairs omitted; roots wrong}\); (B) \(\text{signs wrong}\); (D) \(\text{double counting; }f(1)=-2\ne0\).
Key point: \(\text{factor pairs of }c;\ \text{rational roots }p/q\text{ with }p\mid a_0,\ q\mid a_n\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using the relation between permutations and combinations to solve for n, and evaluating special cases such as nC0, nPn and nCr = nC(n−r)
questions.question: Find \(n\) if \(^nP_4=20\cdot\,^nP_2\). If \(^nC_9=\,^nC_8\), find \(^nC_{17}\). Which special-case statement is correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(n=7;\ ^{17}C_{17}=1;\ \text{special cases correct}\)
Concept: \(\text{arranging }r\text{ chosen objects in }r!\text{ ways gives }^nP_r=r!\,^nC_r;\ \text{choosing }r\text{ is the same as rejecting }n-r\)
Given: \(^nP_4=20\,^nP_2;\ ^nC_9=\,^nC_8\)
Formula/Principle: \(^nP_r=\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!};\ ^nC_a=\,^nC_b\Rightarrow a=b\text{ or }a+b=n\)
Step 1: \(n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)=20n(n-1)\Rightarrow(n-2)(n-3)=20\)
Step 2: \(n^2-5n-14=0\Rightarrow(n-7)(n+2)=0\Rightarrow n=7\)
Step 3: \(9+8=17\Rightarrow n=17;\ ^{17}C_{17}=1\)
Worked derivation: \[^7P_4=840,\ \ ^7P_2=42,\ \ 840=20\times42\]
Check: \[^nP_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}=r!\cdot\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{cancelling the common factor }n(n-1)\text{ reduces the equation to a quadratic}\)
Why not the others: (B) \((4)(3)=12\ne20;\ \text{relation inverted}\); (C) \(0!=1\); (D) \(^nC_r=\,^nC_{n-r}\).
Key point: \(^nP_r=r!\,^nC_r;\ ^nC_r=\,^nC_{n-r}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Evaluating sums of the first n natural numbers, their squares and cubes, using them to sum a series with general term k(k+1), and summing squares over a shifted range
questions.question: Find \(\sum_{k=1}^{10}k,\ \sum_{k=1}^{10}k^2,\ \sum_{k=1}^{10}k^3\), the sum \(1\cdot2+2\cdot3+\dots+10\cdot11\), and \(\sum_{k=11}^{20}k^2\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(55;\ 385;\ 3025;\ 440;\ 2485\)
Concept: \(\sum k=\tfrac{n(n+1)}2,\ \sum k^2=\tfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6,\ \sum k^3=\left[\tfrac{n(n+1)}2\right]^2;\ \text{a series with a polynomial general term splits into these sums}\)
Given: \(n=10;\ k\text{ from }11\text{ to }20\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sum k(k+1)=\sum k^2+\sum k=\dfrac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{3}\)
Step 1: \(\tfrac{10\cdot11}2=55;\ \tfrac{10\cdot11\cdot21}6=385;\ 55^2=3025\)
Step 2: \(385+55=440=\tfrac{10\cdot11\cdot12}{3}\)
Step 3: \(\sum_1^{20}k^2=\tfrac{20\cdot21\cdot41}6=2870\Rightarrow2870-385=2485\)
Worked derivation: \[\sum_{k=1}^n k(k+1)=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6+\frac{n(n+1)}2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+4)}{6}=\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{3}\]
Check: \[\sum k^3=\left(\sum k\right)^2:\ 3025=55^2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a shifted range is a difference of two partial sums}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{series sum and shifted sum wrong}\); (B) \(\sum k^2=385\); (C) \(\sum k=55,\ \sum k^3=3025\).
Key point: \(\sum k^3=(\sum k)^2;\ \sum_{a}^{b}=S_b-S_{a-1}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the perpendicular distance of a point from a line and between parallel lines, converting a line to normal form, and locating points on an axis at a given distance from a line
questions.question: Find the distance of \((3,-5)\) from \(3x-4y-26=0\); the distance between \(3x-4y+7=0\) and \(6x-8y+4=0\); the normal form of \(\sqrt3x+y-8=0\); and the points on the \(x\)-axis at distance 4 from \(4x+3y-12=0\).
options: C) \(\tfrac35;\ \tfrac35;\ p=4,\ \omega=60^\circ;\ (8,0)\text{ only}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\tfrac35;\ 1;\ x\cos30^\circ+y\sin30^\circ=4;\ (8,0),(-2,0)\)
Concept: \(\text{distance of }(x_1,y_1)\text{ from }Ax+By+C=0\text{ is }\dfrac{|Ax_1+By_1+C|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}};\ \text{normal form }x\cos\omega+y\sin\omega=p,\ p>0\)
Given: \(\text{lines and points as stated}\)
Formula/Principle: \(d=\dfrac{|Ax_1+By_1+C|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}};\ d_{\parallel}=\dfrac{|C_1-C_2|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{|9+20-26|}{5}=\dfrac35;\ \text{second line}\equiv3x-4y+2=0\Rightarrow\dfrac{|7-2|}5=1\)
Step 2: \(\text{divide by }\sqrt{3+1}=2:\ \tfrac{\sqrt3}2x+\tfrac12y=4\Rightarrow\omega=30^\circ,\ p=4\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{|4a-12|}{5}=4\Rightarrow4a-12=\pm20\Rightarrow a=8\text{ or }-2\)
Worked derivation: \[\sqrt3x+y=8\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{\sqrt3}{2}x+\frac12y=4\ \Rightarrow\ x\cos30^\circ+y\sin30^\circ=4\]
Check: \[(8,0):\ \frac{|32-12|}{5}=4;\ (-2,0):\ \frac{|-8-12|}{5}=4\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{parallel lines must have identical }A,B\text{ before using }|C_1-C_2|\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{forgot to divide by }\sqrt{A^2+B^2}\); (C) \(\text{second line not normalised; }\omega=30^\circ;\ \text{misses }(-2,0)\); (D) \(\text{sign errors}\).
Key point: \(d=\dfrac{|Ax_1+By_1+C|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Reading semi-axes, eccentricity, foci and latus rectum of an ellipse, the limiting behaviour as eccentricity tends to zero, and finding an ellipse from its foci and major axis
questions.question: For \(\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{y^2}{9}=1\), find the eccentricity, foci and length of latus rectum. What happens to the shape as \(e\to0\)? Find the ellipse with foci \((\pm3,0)\) and major axis 10.
options: A) \(e=\tfrac35;\ (\pm3,0);\ \tfrac{50}{3};\ \text{becomes a line};\ \tfrac{x^2}{25}+\tfrac{y^2}{9}=1\)
B) \(e=\tfrac54;\ (\pm5,0);\ \tfrac{18}{5};\ \text{becomes a parabola};\ \tfrac{x^2}{100}+\tfrac{y^2}{91}=1\)
C) \(e=\tfrac45;\ (\pm4,0);\ \tfrac{18}{5};\ \text{approaches a circle};\ \tfrac{x^2}{25}+\tfrac{y^2}{16}=1\)
D) \(e=\tfrac45;\ (0,\pm4);\ 6;\ \text{approaches a circle};\ \tfrac{x^2}{16}+\tfrac{y^2}{25}=1\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(e=\tfrac45;\ (\pm4,0);\ \text{LR}=\tfrac{18}5;\ \text{circle as }e\to0;\ \tfrac{x^2}{25}+\tfrac{y^2}{16}=1\)
Concept: \(\text{an ellipse is the locus of points whose distances from two foci add to }2a;\ c^2=a^2-b^2,\ e=\tfrac ca<1\)
Given: \(a=5,\ b=3;\ c=3,\ 2a=10\)
Formula/Principle: \(c=\sqrt{a^2-b^2},\ e=\tfrac ca,\ \text{LR}=\tfrac{2b^2}a\)
Step 1: \(c=\sqrt{25-9}=4\Rightarrow e=\tfrac45,\ \text{foci }(\pm4,0)\)
Step 2: \(\text{LR}=\tfrac{2\times9}{5}=\tfrac{18}5;\ e\to0\Rightarrow c\to0,\ b\to a\Rightarrow\text{circle}\)
Step 3: \(a=5,\ c=3\Rightarrow b^2=25-9=16\Rightarrow\tfrac{x^2}{25}+\tfrac{y^2}{16}=1\)
Worked derivation: \[b^2=a^2(1-e^2)\Rightarrow e\to0\Rightarrow b\to a\]
Check: \[\text{point }(0,4):\ \text{distances to }(\pm3,0)\text{ are }5+5=10=2a\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{eccentricity measures how far the foci are from the centre relative to }a\)
Why not the others: (A) \(c=4,\ \text{not }3\); (B) \(e<1\text{ for an ellipse}\); (D) \(\text{major axis is along }x\).
Key point: \(c^2=a^2-b^2,\ e=c/a,\ \text{LR}=2b^2/a\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the equation of a hyperbola from its foci and transverse axis or from its vertices and eccentricity, with its latus rectum and eccentricity
questions.question: Find the hyperbola with foci \((\pm5,0)\) and transverse axis of length 8, its eccentricity and latus rectum. Find also the hyperbola with vertices \((0,\pm3)\) and eccentricity \(\tfrac53\).
options: A) \(\tfrac{x^2}{16}-\tfrac{y^2}{9}=1;\ e=\tfrac54;\ \text{LR}=\tfrac92;\ \tfrac{y^2}{9}-\tfrac{x^2}{16}=1\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\tfrac{x^2}{16}-\tfrac{y^2}{9}=1,\ e=\tfrac54,\ \text{LR}=\tfrac92;\ \tfrac{y^2}9-\tfrac{x^2}{16}=1\)
Concept: \(\text{a hyperbola is the locus of points whose distances from two foci differ by }2a;\ c^2=a^2+b^2,\ e=\tfrac ca>1\)
Given: \(c=5,\ 2a=8;\ a=3\ (\text{vertical}),\ e=\tfrac53\)
Formula/Principle: \(b^2=c^2-a^2;\ \text{LR}=\tfrac{2b^2}{a}\)
Step 1: \(a=4,\ b^2=25-16=9\Rightarrow\tfrac{x^2}{16}-\tfrac{y^2}9=1\)
Step 2: \(e=\tfrac54;\ \text{LR}=\tfrac{2\times9}{4}=\tfrac92\)
Step 3: \(c=ae=5\Rightarrow b^2=25-9=16\Rightarrow\tfrac{y^2}{9}-\tfrac{x^2}{16}=1\)
Worked derivation: \[b^2=a^2(e^2-1)=9\left(\frac{25}{9}-1\right)=16\]
Check: \[\text{vertex }(4,0):\ |9-1|=8=2a\ \text{(distances to foci }(\pm5,0))\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{for a hyperbola }c>a,\ \text{so }b^2=c^2-a^2\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{that is an ellipse}\); (C) \(a=4,\ \text{not }5\); (D) \(a\text{ and }b\text{ swapped}\).
Key point: \(c^2=a^2+b^2;\ e>1;\ \text{LR}=2b^2/a\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Differentiating with product, quotient and chain rules and using the derivative to find where x e^(−x) increases, decreases and attains its maximum
questions.question: Find \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin(x^2)\) and \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\dfrac{x^2}{x+1}\). For \(f(x)=xe^{-x}\), find the interval where \(f\) increases and its maximum value.
options: A) \(\cos(x^2);\ \dfrac{2x}{1};\ \text{increasing everywhere}\)
D) \(2x\cos(x^2);\ \dfrac{x^2+2x}{(x+1)^2};\ \text{increasing on }(-\infty,1),\ \text{maximum }f(1)=\tfrac1e\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(2x\cos(x^2);\ \dfrac{x^2+2x}{(x+1)^2};\ \text{increasing on }(-\infty,1),\ \max\tfrac1e\)
Concept: \((uv)'=u'v+uv';\ \left(\tfrac uv\right)'=\tfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2};\ \tfrac{d}{dx}f(g(x))=f'(g(x))g'(x)\)
Given: \(\sin(x^2),\ \tfrac{x^2}{x+1},\ xe^{-x}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{chain, quotient and product rules}\)
Step 1: \(\cos(x^2)\cdot2x\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{2x(x+1)-x^2}{(x+1)^2}=\dfrac{x^2+2x}{(x+1)^2}\)
Step 3: \(f'(x)=e^{-x}-xe^{-x}=e^{-x}(1-x)>0\iff x<1;\ f(1)=e^{-1}\)
Worked derivation: \[f'(x)=e^{-x}(1-x):\ +\ \text{for }x<1,\ -\ \text{for }x>1\Rightarrow\text{maximum at }x=1\]
Check: \[f(0)=0,\ f(1)=0.368,\ f(2)=0.271\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(e^{-x}>0\text{ always, so the sign of }f'\text{ is the sign of }1-x\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{inner derivatives missing}\); (B) \(\text{chain rule misapplied; sign wrong}\); (C) \(\text{signs and denominator wrong}\).
Key point: \(\text{chain: multiply by the inner derivative};\ \text{sign of }f'\text{ gives monotonicity}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Applying Bayes theorem to find the probability that a defective item came from a particular machine, together with the total probability of a defective item
questions.question: Machines A and B produce 60% and 40% of a factory's bolts; 2% of A's and 3% of B's bolts are defective. A bolt is picked at random. Find the probability that it is defective, and the probability that a defective bolt came from A. Are the two machines equally likely sources of a defective bolt?
options: B) \(0.024;\ 0.5;\ \text{yes — A's larger output exactly balances its lower defect rate}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(P(D)=0.024;\ P(A\mid D)=0.5;\ \text{equally likely}\)
Concept: \(P(E_i\mid A)=\dfrac{P(E_i)P(A\mid E_i)}{\sum_jP(E_j)P(A\mid E_j)}\ \text{revises prior probabilities after an observation}\)
Given: \(P(A)=0.6,\ P(B)=0.4,\ P(D\mid A)=0.02,\ P(D\mid B)=0.03\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Bayes theorem with total probability in the denominator}\)
Step 1: \(P(D)=0.6\times0.02+0.4\times0.03=0.012+0.012=0.024\)
Step 2: \(P(A\mid D)=\dfrac{0.012}{0.024}=0.5\)
Step 3: \(P(B\mid D)=0.5\Rightarrow\text{equal}\)
Worked derivation: \[P(A\mid D)=\frac{0.6\times0.02}{0.6\times0.02+0.4\times0.03}=\frac{0.012}{0.024}=\frac12\]
Check: \[P(A\mid D)+P(B\mid D)=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the posterior weight of each machine is its share of all defective bolts}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{rates added without weights}\); (C) \(\text{prior used as posterior}\); (D) \(P(D)\text{ omits B's share}\).
Key point: \(P(E_i|A)\propto P(E_i)P(A|E_i)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving an equation in inverse tangents and rejecting extraneous roots by principal-value ranges, and evaluating inverse cosine and sine of angles outside the principal range
questions.question: Solve \(\tan^{-1}(x+1)+\tan^{-1}(x-1)=\tan^{-1}\tfrac{8}{31}\). Evaluate \(\cos^{-1}\!\left(\cos\tfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)\) and \(\sin^{-1}\!\left(\sin\tfrac{3\pi}{5}\right)\).
options: A) \(x=\tfrac14\text{ only (}x=-8\text{ makes the left side negative)};\ \tfrac{5\pi}6;\ \tfrac{2\pi}5\)
B) \(x=\tfrac14\text{ or }-8;\ \tfrac{7\pi}6;\ \tfrac{3\pi}5\)
D) \(x=4;\ \tfrac\pi6;\ \tfrac{3\pi}5\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(x=\tfrac14;\ \tfrac{5\pi}6;\ \tfrac{2\pi}5\)
Concept: \(\tan^{-1}a+\tan^{-1}b=\tan^{-1}\frac{a+b}{1-ab}\text{ only when }ab<1;\ \cos^{-1}\text{ has range }[0,\pi]\text{ and }\sin^{-1}\text{ has range }[-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2]\)
Given: \(\tan^{-1}(x+1)+\tan^{-1}(x-1)=\tan^{-1}\tfrac{8}{31}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{(x+1)+(x-1)}{1-(x^2-1)}=\dfrac{2x}{2-x^2}=\dfrac{8}{31}\)
Step 1: \(62x=16-8x^2\Rightarrow4x^2+31x-8=0\Rightarrow(4x-1)(x+8)=0\)
Step 2: \(x=-8:\ \tan^{-1}(-7)+\tan^{-1}(-9)<0\text{ but }\tan^{-1}\tfrac8{31}>0\Rightarrow\text{reject};\ x=\tfrac14\text{ valid}\)
Step 3: \(\cos\tfrac{7\pi}6=\cos\tfrac{5\pi}6\Rightarrow\tfrac{5\pi}6;\ \sin\tfrac{3\pi}5=\sin\tfrac{2\pi}5\Rightarrow\tfrac{2\pi}5\)
Worked derivation: \[x=\tfrac14:\ \tan^{-1}\tfrac54+\tan^{-1}\left(-\tfrac34\right)=\tan^{-1}\frac{\frac54-\frac34}{1+\frac{15}{16}}=\tan^{-1}\frac{1/2}{31/16}=\tan^{-1}\frac{8}{31}\]
Check: \[ab=\tfrac54\cdot\left(-\tfrac34\right)=-\tfrac{15}{16}<1\ \text{so the formula applies};\ \tfrac{5\pi}{6}\in[0,\pi],\ \tfrac{2\pi}{5}\in\left[-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2\right]\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{principal-value ranges decide which algebraic root and which angle are acceptable}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(x=-8\text{ is extraneous; angles outside principal ranges}\); (C) \(\text{wrong root and signs}\); (D) \(\text{not a root; values wrong}\).
Key point: \(\text{check roots against principal ranges}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Showing with 2×2 matrices that AB can be zero while neither factor is zero and that AB need not equal BA, and that (A+B)² differs from A² + 2AB + B²
questions.question: Let \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix},\ B=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\). Find \(AB\), \(BA\), \(A^2\), and compare \((A+B)^2\) with \(A^2+2AB+B^2\).
options: A) \(AB=BA=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix};\ A^2=A;\ \text{equal}\)
B) \(AB=O,\ BA=O;\ A^2=O;\ \text{equal}\)
C) \(AB=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix},\ BA=O;\ A^2=I;\ \text{equal}\)

D) \(AB=O,\ BA= egin{bmatrix}0&1\0&0\end{bmatrix}\ (	ext{so }AB
e BA	ext{ and }AB=O	ext{ with }A,B
e O);\ A^2=O;\ (A+B)^2= egin{bmatrix}1&1\0&0\end{bmatrix}
e A^2+2AB+B^2= egin{bmatrix}1&0\0&0\end{bmatrix}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(AB=O\ne BA;\ A^2=O;\ (A+B)^2\ne A^2+2AB+B^2\)
Concept: \(\text{matrix multiplication is not commutative, and the product of two non-zero matrices can be the zero matrix, so algebraic identities like }(a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2\text{ fail}\)
Given: \(A,B\text{ as stated}\)
Formula/Principle: \((A+B)^2=A^2+AB+BA+B^2\)
Step 1: \(AB=\begin{bmatrix}0\cdot1+1\cdot0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}=O;\ BA=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(A^2=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}=O;\ B^2=B\)
Step 3: \(A+B=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix},\ (A+B)^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix};\ A^2+2AB+B^2=B\)
Worked derivation: \[(A+B)^2-(A^2+2AB+B^2)=BA-AB=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\ne O\]
Check: \[\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the cross terms are }AB+BA,\ \text{which equals }2AB\text{ only if }A\text{ and }B\text{ commute}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(AB=O;\ A^2=O\); (B) \(BA\ne O\); (C) \(\text{products swapped; }A^2=O\).
Key point: \(AB\ne BA\text{ in general};\ AB=O\not\Rightarrow A=O\text{ or }B=O\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding first and second derivatives of a parametrically defined ellipse, locating its horizontal tangent, and finding where the curve x = t + 1/t, y = t − 1/t has vertical tangents
questions.question: For the ellipse \(x=3\cos t,\ y=2\sin t\), find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(t=\tfrac\pi4\) and the point with a horizontal tangent for \(0<t<\pi\). For \(x=t+\tfrac1t,\ y=t-\tfrac1t\), find \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) and where the tangent is vertical.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(-\tfrac23;\ -\tfrac{4\sqrt2}9;\ (0,2);\ \dfrac{t^2+1}{t^2-1};\ \text{vertical at }t=\pm1\)
Concept: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt};\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{dx/dt};\ \text{horizontal tangent when }dy/dt=0,\ \text{vertical when }dx/dt=0\)
Given: \(x=3\cos t,\ y=2\sin t;\ x=t+\tfrac1t,\ y=t-\tfrac1t\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{parametric differentiation}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2\cos t}{-3\sin t}=-\tfrac23\cot t\Rightarrow-\tfrac23\text{ at }\tfrac\pi4\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{\frac23\csc^2t}{-3\sin t}=-\tfrac29\csc^3t=-\tfrac29(2\sqrt2)=-\tfrac{4\sqrt2}9;\ \cos t=0\Rightarrow t=\tfrac\pi2,\ (0,2)\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1+1/t^2}{1-1/t^2}=\dfrac{t^2+1}{t^2-1};\ dx/dt=0\Rightarrow t=\pm1\Rightarrow(\pm2,0)\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{d}{dt}\left(-\tfrac23\cot t\right)=\tfrac23\csc^2t,\quad\frac{dx}{dt}=-3\sin t\]
Check: \[x^2-y^2=\left(t+\tfrac1t\right)^2-\left(t-\tfrac1t\right)^2=4\Rightarrow\text{hyperbola with vertices }(\pm2,0)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the second derivative must be divided by }dx/dt\text{ again, not just differentiated in }t\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ratio inverted}\); (C) \(\text{sign and second derivative wrong}\); (D) \(\text{second derivative not divided by }dx/dt\).
Key point: \(y''=\dfrac{d(y')/dt}{dx/dt}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Maximising the volume of an open box made by cutting equal squares from the corners of a square sheet, and maximising the area of a rectangle of fixed perimeter
questions.question: Equal squares of side \(x\) are cut from the corners of an 18 cm square sheet, and the sides are folded up to make an open box. Find \(x\) for maximum volume and the maximum volume. What is the largest area of a rectangle with perimeter 40 cm?
options: A) \(x=3\text{ cm};\ 432\text{ cm}^3;\ 100\text{ cm}^2\ (\text{a square of side }10\text{ cm})\)
C) \(x=6\text{ cm};\ 216\text{ cm}^3;\ 96\text{ cm}^2\)
D) \(x=2\text{ cm};\ 392\text{ cm}^3;\ 100\text{ cm}^2\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(x=3\text{ cm};\ V_{\max}=432\text{ cm}^3;\ 100\text{ cm}^2\)
Concept: \(\text{express the quantity in one variable, set the derivative to zero and confirm a maximum with the second derivative}\)
Given: \(\text{sheet }18\text{ cm};\ \text{perimeter }40\text{ cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(V=x(18-2x)^2,\ 0<x<9;\ A=l(20-l)\)
Step 1: \(V'=(18-2x)^2-4x(18-2x)=(18-2x)(18-6x)\)
Step 2: \(V'=0\Rightarrow x=3\ (x=9\text{ gives }V=0);\ V(3)=3\times12^2=432\)
Step 3: \(A'=20-2l=0\Rightarrow l=10\Rightarrow A=100\text{ cm}^2\)
Worked derivation: \[V''=24x-144\Rightarrow V''(3)=-72<0\Rightarrow\text{maximum}\]
Check: \[V(2)=2\times14^2=392<432,\ \ V(4)=4\times10^2=400<432\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{cutting too little gives a shallow box and too much a narrow one; the optimum balances them}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(x=9\text{ gives no base}\); (C) \(V(6)=216<432\); (D) \(V(2)=392\text{ is not the maximum}\).
Key point: \(V'=0,\ V''<0\Rightarrow\text{maximum}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Integrating standard forms with quadratic denominators and square roots, completing the square, and finding an unknown limit from the value of a definite integral
questions.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2+4}\), \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\) and \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2+2x+5}\). Find \(a>0\) if \(\displaystyle\int_0^a\frac{dx}{x^2+9}=\frac{\pi}{12}\).
options: C) \(\tfrac12\tan^{-1}\tfrac x2+C;\ \sin^{-1}\tfrac x3+C;\ \tfrac12\tan^{-1}\tfrac{x+1}2+C;\ a=3\)
D) \(2\tan^{-1}\tfrac x2;\ \sin^{-1}\tfrac x3;\ \tfrac12\tan^{-1}\tfrac{x+1}{2};\ a=\sqrt3\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\tfrac12\tan^{-1}\tfrac x2;\ \sin^{-1}\tfrac x3;\ \tfrac12\tan^{-1}\tfrac{x+1}2;\ a=3\)
Concept: \(\int\frac{dx}{x^2+a^2}=\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac xa;\ \int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}=\sin^{-1}\frac xa;\ \text{complete the square to reach a standard form}\)
Given: \(a=2,\ 3;\ x^2+2x+5=(x+1)^2+4\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{standard integrals}\)
Step 1: \(\tfrac12\tan^{-1}\tfrac x2;\ \sin^{-1}\tfrac x3\)
Step 2: \(\int\frac{dx}{(x+1)^2+2^2}=\tfrac12\tan^{-1}\tfrac{x+1}2\)
Step 3: \(\tfrac13\tan^{-1}\tfrac a3=\tfrac\pi{12}\Rightarrow\tan^{-1}\tfrac a3=\tfrac\pi4\Rightarrow a=3\)
Worked derivation: \[\int_0^a\frac{dx}{x^2+9}=\left[\frac13\tan^{-1}\frac x3\right]_0^a=\frac13\tan^{-1}\frac a3\]
Check: \[\frac{d}{dx}\left[\tfrac12\tan^{-1}\tfrac x2\right]=\frac12\cdot\frac{1/2}{1+x^2/4}=\frac{1}{x^2+4}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the factor }\tfrac1a\text{ comes from the chain rule on }\tan^{-1}(x/a)\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{missing }\tfrac1a\text{ and scaling}\); (B) \(\text{log form is for }x\,dx;\ a\text{ wrong}\); (D) \(\text{factor should be }\tfrac12\).
Key point: \(\int\frac{dx}{x^2+a^2}=\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac xa\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Differentiating integrals with variable limits using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and evaluating a limit of an average of an integral as the interval shrinks
questions.question: Find \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\displaystyle\int_0^x e^{-t^2}dt\), \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\displaystyle\int_x^{x^2}\frac{dt}{t}\ (x>0)\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac1x\int_0^x\sec^2t\,dt\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(e^{-x^2};\ \tfrac1x;\ 1\)
Concept: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\int_{a(x)}^{b(x)}f(t)\,dt=f(b(x))b'(x)-f(a(x))a'(x);\ \text{the average of a continuous }f\text{ over }[0,x]\text{ tends to }f(0)\)
Given: \(f(t)=e^{-t^2},\ \tfrac1t,\ \sec^2t\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Leibniz form)}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\int_0^xe^{-t^2}dt=e^{-x^2}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\cdot2x-\dfrac1x\cdot1=\dfrac2x-\dfrac1x=\dfrac1x\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac1x\int_0^x\sec^2t\,dt=\dfrac{\tan x}{x}\to1\)
Worked derivation: \[\int_x^{x^2}\frac{dt}{t}=\ln x^2-\ln x=\ln x\Rightarrow\frac{d}{dx}\ln x=\frac1x\]
Check: \[\sec^2 0=1=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\tan x}{x}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the derivative of an accumulation function is the integrand at the moving limit, times that limit's derivative}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{evaluated instead of differentiated}\); (B) \(\text{differentiated the integrand; chain factor missing}\); (D) \(\text{variable not replaced; lower limit ignored}\).
Key point: \(\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^{g(x)}f=f(g(x))g'(x)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving linear first-order equations in the forms dy/dx + Py = Q and dx/dy + Px = Q with integrating factors and finding particular solutions from given conditions
questions.question: Solve \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}+y=e^{-x}\) with \(y(0)=1\). Solve \(y\,dx-(x+2y^2)\,dy=0\) and find the particular solution with \(x=2\) when \(y=1\).
options: D) \(y=(x+1)e^{-x};\ x=2y^2+Cy\ (\text{using }\tfrac{dx}{dy}-\tfrac xy=2y,\ \text{IF}=\tfrac1y);\ x=2y^2\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(y=(x+1)e^{-x};\ x=2y^2+Cy;\ x=2y^2\)
Concept: \(\text{for }\frac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q,\ \text{IF}=e^{\int P\,dx}\text{ and }y\cdot\text{IF}=\int Q\cdot\text{IF}\,dx;\ \text{if the equation is linear in }x,\ \text{use }\frac{dx}{dy}+P_1x=Q_1\text{ with IF}=e^{\int P_1dy}\)
Given: \(P=1,\ Q=e^{-x};\ \tfrac{dx}{dy}=\tfrac{x+2y^2}{y}\)
Formula/Principle: \(y\cdot\text{IF}=\int Q\cdot\text{IF}\,dx\)
Step 1: \(\text{IF}=e^x:\ ye^x=\int1\,dx=x+C;\ y(0)=1\Rightarrow C=1\Rightarrow y=(x+1)e^{-x}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dx}{dy}-\dfrac1yx=2y;\ \text{IF}=e^{-\ln y}=\tfrac1y:\ \tfrac xy=\int2\,dy=2y+C\)
Step 3: \(x=2y^2+Cy;\ (2,1):\ 2=2+C\Rightarrow C=0\Rightarrow x=2y^2\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{d}{dy}\left(\frac xy\right)=\frac1y\frac{dx}{dy}-\frac{x}{y^2}=\frac1y\left(\frac{dx}{dy}-\frac xy\right)=2\]
Check: \[y=(x+1)e^{-x}:\ y'+y=e^{-x}-(x+1)e^{-x}+(x+1)e^{-x}=e^{-x}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the second equation is linear in }x\text{ (not in }y),\ \text{so }y\text{ is taken as the independent variable}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{misses the }xe^{-x}\text{ term; coefficient wrong}\); (B) \(\text{sign of exponent wrong; }C\text{ multiplies }y\); (C) \(\text{initial condition fails; variables swapped}\).
Key point: \(\text{IF}=e^{\int P};\ \text{use }dx/dy\text{ form when linear in }x\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Computing a cross product to find areas of a parallelogram and triangle and a unit normal, and finding an unknown component that gives a required area
questions.question: For \(\vec a=\hat i+\hat j-\hat k\) and \(\vec b=\hat i-\hat j+\hat k\), find \(\vec a\times\vec b\), the area of the parallelogram and of the triangle they determine, and a unit vector perpendicular to both. Find \(\lambda\) if \(\vec p=\hat i+\lambda\hat j\) and \(\vec q=\hat i-\hat j\) span a parallelogram of area 3.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\vec a\times\vec b=(0,-2,-2);\ 2\sqrt2;\ \sqrt2;\ \pm\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(0,1,1);\ \lambda=2,-4\)
Concept: \(|\vec a\times\vec b|\text{ is the area of the parallelogram on }\vec a,\vec b;\ \text{half of it is the triangle};\ \vec a\times\vec b\text{ is perpendicular to both}\)
Given: \(\vec a=(1,1,-1),\ \vec b=(1,-1,1);\ \vec p=(1,\lambda,0),\ \vec q=(1,-1,0)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\vec a\times\vec b=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\a_1&a_2&a_3\\b_1&b_2&b_3\end{vmatrix}\)
Step 1: \(\hat i(1-1)-\hat j(1+1)+\hat k(-1-1)=(0,-2,-2)\)
Step 2: \(|\vec a\times\vec b|=\sqrt8=2\sqrt2;\ \text{triangle }\sqrt2;\ \text{unit normal }\pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(0,1,1)\)
Step 3: \(\vec p\times\vec q=(0,0,-1-\lambda)\Rightarrow|1+\lambda|=3\Rightarrow\lambda=2\text{ or }-4\)
Worked derivation: \[\vec p\times\vec q=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&\lambda&0\\1&-1&0\end{vmatrix}=\hat k(-1-\lambda)\]
Check: \[(0,-2,-2)\cdot(1,1,-1)=0-2+2=0;\ \ (0,-2,-2)\cdot(1,-1,1)=0+2-2=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the magnitude of the cross product is }|\vec a||\vec b|\sin\theta,\ \text{the base times height}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{sign and magnitude wrong; one value of }\lambda\text{ only}\); (B) \(\text{cross product wrong}\); (D) \(\text{used }|\cdot|^2;\ \text{not unit; misses }\lambda=-4\).
Key point: \(\text{area}=|\vec a\times\vec b|;\ \text{triangle}=\tfrac12|\vec a\times\vec b|\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the shortest distance between two skew lines in vector form and the angle between them using their direction vectors
questions.question: Find the shortest distance between \(\vec r=(\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k)+\lambda(\hat i-3\hat j+2\hat k)\) and \(\vec r=(4\hat i+5\hat j+6\hat k)+\mu(2\hat i+3\hat j+\hat k)\), and the cosine of the angle between them.
options: A) \(0\ (\text{they intersect});\ \tfrac{5}{14}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(d=\tfrac{3}{\sqrt{19}};\ \cos\theta=\tfrac5{14}\)
Concept: \(\text{for skew lines }\vec r=\vec a_1+\lambda\vec b_1,\ \vec r=\vec a_2+\mu\vec b_2,\ d=\dfrac{|(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)\cdot(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}\)
Given: \(\vec a_1=(1,2,3),\ \vec b_1=(1,-3,2),\ \vec a_2=(4,5,6),\ \vec b_2=(2,3,1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(d=\dfrac{|(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)\cdot(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|};\ \cos\theta=\dfrac{|\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2|}{|\vec b_1||\vec b_2|}\)
Step 1: \(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=(-3-6,\ -(1-4),\ 3+6)=(-9,3,9),\ |\cdot|=\sqrt{171}=3\sqrt{19}\)
Step 2: \(\vec a_2-\vec a_1=(3,3,3);\ (-9,3,9)\cdot(3,3,3)=-27+9+27=9\Rightarrow d=\dfrac{9}{3\sqrt{19}}=\dfrac3{\sqrt{19}}\)
Step 3: \(\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2=2-9+2=-5;\ |\vec b_1|=|\vec b_2|=\sqrt{14}\Rightarrow\cos\theta=\tfrac5{14}\)
Worked derivation: \[\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&-3&2\\2&3&1\end{vmatrix}=-9\hat i+3\hat j+9\hat k\]
Check: \[(-9,3,9)\cdot(1,-3,2)=-9-9+18=0;\ \ (-9,3,9)\cdot(2,3,1)=-18+9+9=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the common perpendicular is along }\vec b_1\times\vec b_2,\ \text{and projecting the joining vector onto it gives the gap}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(d\ne0,\ \text{so they do not meet}\); (C) \(\text{used }|\vec a_2-\vec a_1|\); (D) \(\text{angle between lines uses }|\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2|\text{ and }\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2=-5\).
Key point: \(d=\dfrac{|(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)\cdot(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Ordering the electromagnetic spectrum with sources and uses of each band, and using energy conservation to find the shortest X-ray wavelength produced by electrons accelerated through a given voltage
questions.question: Electrons accelerated through \(30\text{ kV}\) strike a metal target in an X-ray tube (\(hc=1240\text{ eV nm}\)). Find the shortest X-ray wavelength produced. Which matching of bands with sources and uses is correct?
options: A) \(0.0413\text{ nm};\ \text{radio waves from accelerated charges in antennas (communication)};\ \text{microwaves from klystron or magnetron valves (radar, ovens)};\ \text{infrared from hot bodies (remote controls, greenhouse effect)};\ \text{ultraviolet from the Sun and arc lamps (sterilising water)};\ \text{X-rays from fast electrons striking metal (medical diagnosis)};\ \gamma\text{-rays from nuclei (cancer treatment)}\)
B) \(41.3\text{ nm};\ \text{X-rays come from radioactive nuclei; radio waves from hot bodies}\)
C) \(0.0413\text{ nm};\ \text{infrared is used in radar; microwaves in X-ray imaging}\)
D) \(1240\text{ nm};\ \gamma\text{-rays have the longest wavelength}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\lambda_{\min}\approx0.0413\text{ nm};\ \text{sources and uses correctly matched}\)
Given: \(V=30\text{ kV}\Rightarrow K=30\text{ keV}\)
Formula/Principle: \(eV=h\nu_{\max}=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{\min}}\ (\text{all kinetic energy into one photon})\)
Step 1: \(\lambda_{\min}=\dfrac{1240\text{ eV nm}}{30\,000\text{ eV}}\)
Step 2: \(\lambda_{\min}=0.0413\text{ nm}\)
Step 3: \(\text{order of increasing }\lambda:\ \gamma<\text{X}<\text{UV}<\text{visible}<\text{IR}<\text{micro}<\text{radio}\)
Worked derivation: \[eV=\frac{hc}{\lambda_{\min}}\Rightarrow\lambda_{\min}=\frac{hc}{eV}=\frac{1240}{3.0\times10^4}\ \text{nm}\]
Check: \[0.0413\ \text{nm lies in the X-ray band }(\sim10^{-3}\text{ to }10\ \text{nm})\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{an electron can give at most all its kinetic energy to a single photon}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{factor }10^3\text{ error; sources swapped}\); (C) \(\text{uses swapped}\); (D) \(\gamma\text{-rays have the shortest wavelength}\).
Key point: \(\lambda_{\min}=hc/eV;\ \text{spectrum order by wavelength}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding refractive index from the angle of minimum deviation, deviation by a thin prism, dispersion of colours, and the limiting change when the prism is immersed in water
questions.question: An equilateral glass prism (\(A=60^\circ\)) gives minimum deviation \(30^\circ\). Find its refractive index. A thin prism of angle \(5^\circ\) has \(n=1.5\); find its deviation. Which colour deviates most, and how does the deviation change if the prism is placed in water?
options: A) \(1.5;\ 7.5^\circ;\ \text{red};\ \text{increases}\)
B) \(\sqrt2\approx1.41;\ 2.5^\circ;\ \text{violet (largest }n);\ \text{decreases, since the relative index }n_{\text{glass}}/n_{\text{water}}\text{ is smaller}\)
C) \(2;\ 5^\circ;\ \text{violet};\ \text{unchanged}\)
D) \(1.22;\ 2.5^\circ;\ \text{red};\ \text{decreases to zero}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(n=\sqrt2;\ \delta=2.5^\circ;\ \text{violet};\ \text{deviation decreases in water}\)
Given: \(A=60^\circ,\ D_m=30^\circ;\ A'=5^\circ,\ n'=1.5\)
Formula/Principle: \(n=\dfrac{\sin\frac{A+D_m}{2}}{\sin\frac A2};\ \delta=(n-1)A\ \text{(thin prism)}\)
Step 1: \(n=\dfrac{\sin45^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}=\dfrac{0.707}{0.5}=\sqrt2\)
Step 2: \(\delta=(1.5-1)\times5^\circ=2.5^\circ\)
Step 3: \(n_{\text{violet}}>n_{\text{red}}\Rightarrow\delta_{\text{violet}}\text{ largest};\ \text{in water }n_{\text{rel}}=\tfrac{1.5}{1.33}\approx1.13\Rightarrow\delta\approx0.13A\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{at minimum deviation } r_1=r_2=\frac A2,\ i=\frac{A+D_m}{2}\Rightarrow n=\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}\]
Check: \[\delta_{\text{water}}=(1.13-1)\times5^\circ\approx0.6^\circ<2.5^\circ\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{deviation depends on the refractive index of the prism relative to its surroundings}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{formula misapplied; violet deviates most}\); (C) \(\text{index wrong; deviation changes in water}\); (D) \(\text{index wrong; violet deviates most}\).
Key point: \(n=\sin\frac{A+D_m}2/\sin\frac A2;\ \delta=(n-1)A\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Explaining why coherent sources are needed for a sustained interference pattern and calculating maximum-to-minimum intensity ratio and intensity at a given path difference
questions.question: Two slits give individual intensities in the ratio \(9:1\) on a screen. Find the ratio of maximum to minimum intensity in the interference pattern. If two coherent waves of equal intensity \(I_0\) meet with a path difference \(\lambda/3\), what is the resultant intensity? Why do two separate bulbs not produce a sustained pattern?
options: A) \(9:1;\ 2I_0;\ \text{bulbs are too far apart}\)
B) \(10:8;\ 3I_0;\ \text{bulbs emit only one wavelength}\)

C) \(4:1\ (\text{amplitudes }3:1\Rightarrow(3+1)^2:(3-1)^2=16:4);\ I_0\ (\phi=\tfrac{2\pi}3,\ I=4I_0\cos^2\tfrac\pi3);\ \text{independent sources change phase randomly in less than }10^{-8}\text{ s, so the pattern averages out; coherent sources (derived from one source as in Young's experiment) keep a constant phase difference}\)
D) \(16:4;\ 4I_0;\ \text{intensity always adds}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(I_{\max}:I_{\min}=4:1;\ I=I_0;\ \text{coherence needed for a sustained pattern}\)
Given: \(I_1:I_2=9:1;\ \Delta x=\lambda/3\)
Formula/Principle: \(a\propto\sqrt I;\ I_{\max}=(a_1+a_2)^2,\ I_{\min}=(a_1-a_2)^2;\ \phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x;\ I=4I_0\cos^2\dfrac\phi2\)
Step 1: \(a_1:a_2=3:1\Rightarrow I_{\max}:I_{\min}=16:4=4:1\)
Step 2: \(\phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\Rightarrow\cos^2\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac14\)
Step 3: \(I=4I_0\times\tfrac14=I_0\)
Worked derivation: \[I=I_1+I_2+2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi=I_0+I_0+2I_0\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}=2I_0-I_0=I_0\]
Check: \[\frac{(3+1)^2}{(3-1)^2}=\frac{16}{4}=4\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a stationary pattern needs a phase difference that stays fixed in time}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{intensities, not amplitudes, used; result wrong}\); (B) \(\text{ratio and intensity wrong}\); (D) \(\text{unsimplified ratio; phase ignored}\).
Key point: \(I_{\max}/I_{\min}=\left(\frac{\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2}}{\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2}}\right)^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the radius, speed and kinetic, potential and total energies of the electron in the third Bohr orbit of hydrogen and the energy to ionise from that orbit, compared with measured ionisation energy
questions.question: The measured ionisation energy of hydrogen is \(13.6\text{ eV}\). Using the Bohr model (\(r_1=0.529\text{ Å},\ v_1=2.18\times10^6\text{ m s}^{-1}\)), find for \(n=3\) the orbit radius, electron speed, total energy, kinetic and potential energies, and the energy needed to ionise from this level.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(r_3=4.76\text{ Å};\ v_3=7.27\times10^5\text{ m s}^{-1};\ E_3=-1.51\text{ eV};\ K=1.51,\ U=-3.02\text{ eV};\ 1.51\text{ eV}\)
Given: \(n=3;\ r_1=0.529\text{ Å},\ v_1=2.18\times10^6\text{ m s}^{-1},\ E_1=-13.6\text{ eV}\)
Formula/Principle: \(r_n=n^2r_1;\ v_n=\dfrac{v_1}{n};\ E_n=\dfrac{E_1}{n^2};\ K=-E,\ U=2E\)
Step 1: \(r_3=9\times0.529=4.76\text{ Å}\)
Step 2: \(v_3=\dfrac{2.18\times10^6}{3}=7.27\times10^5\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Step 3: \(E_3=-\dfrac{13.6}{9}=-1.51\text{ eV}\Rightarrow K=1.51,\ U=-3.02\text{ eV};\ \text{ionisation energy from }n=3:\ 1.51\text{ eV}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{ke^2}{r^2}\Rightarrow K=\frac{ke^2}{2r}=-\frac{U}{2}\Rightarrow E=K+U=-K\]
Check: \[K+U=1.51-3.02=-1.51\ \text{eV}=E_3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{in a Coulomb orbit the kinetic energy is half the magnitude of the potential energy}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{used }n\text{ instead of }n^2\text{ and }1/n\); (B) \(\text{radius divided; signs of }K,U\text{ reversed}\); (C) \(\text{values of }n=1\).
Key point: \(r\propto n^2,\ v\propto1/n,\ E\propto-1/n^2;\ K=-E,\ U=2E\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating mass defect and binding energy per nucleon for the deuteron and oxygen-16 from atomic masses and comparing their stability
questions.question: Using \(m(^1\text{H})=1.007825\text{ u},\ m_n=1.008665\text{ u},\ m(^2\text{H})=2.014102\text{ u},\ m(^{16}\text{O})=15.994915\text{ u}\) and \(1\text{ u}=931.5\text{ MeV}/c^2\), find the binding energy per nucleon of the deuteron and of \(^{16}\text{O}\). Which is more stable?
options: A) \(2.22\text{ MeV};\ 127.6\text{ MeV};\ \text{deuteron, since its total binding energy is less}\)
B) \(1.11\text{ MeV};\ 7.98\text{ MeV};\ \text{the deuteron is more stable}\)
C) \(0.0024\text{ u};\ 0.137\text{ u};\ \text{equally stable}\)
D) \(\approx1.11\text{ MeV};\ \approx7.98\text{ MeV};\ ^{16}\text{O is much more stable, since a higher binding energy per nucleon means more energy is needed per nucleon to pull the nucleus apart}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\approx1.11\text{ vs }\approx7.98\text{ MeV per nucleon};\ ^{16}\text{O far more stable}\)
Given: \(\text{atomic masses as stated}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta m=Zm_H+(A-Z)m_n-M;\ E_b=\Delta m\times931.5\text{ MeV};\ E_{bn}=E_b/A\)
Step 1: \(\text{deuteron: }\Delta m=1.007825+1.008665-2.014102=0.002388\text{ u}\Rightarrow E_b=2.224\text{ MeV}\Rightarrow1.11\text{ MeV/nucleon}\)
Step 2: \(^{16}\text{O}:\ \Delta m=8(1.007825)+8(1.008665)-15.994915=0.137005\text{ u}\)
Step 3: \(E_b=0.137005\times931.5=127.6\text{ MeV}\Rightarrow127.6/16=7.98\text{ MeV/nucleon}\)
Worked derivation: \[8m_H+8m_n=8.0626+8.06932=16.13192\ \text{u};\ \ 16.13192-15.994915=0.137005\ \text{u}\]
Check: \[7.98\ \text{MeV close to the plateau value }\approx8\ \text{MeV for medium nuclei}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{stability is judged by binding energy per nucleon, not by the total}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{total binding energies quoted; deuteron is less stable}\); (B) \(\text{conclusion reversed}\); (C) \(\text{mass defects, not energies}\).
Key point: \(E_{bn}=\Delta m\,c^2/A;\ \text{larger }E_{bn}\Rightarrow\text{more stable}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Applying significant-figure rules to addition and multiplication, counting significant figures in given measurements, and rounding off when the dropped digit is 5
questions.question: Give the results with correct significant figures: (i) \(3.42+15.7+0.128\); (ii) \(2.5\times3.142\). How many significant figures are in \(0.03040\) and \(5.000\times10^3\)? Round \(6.375\) and \(6.365\) to three significant figures.
options: B) \(19.2;\ 7.9;\ 4;\ 4;\ 6.38,\ 6.36\ (\text{when the dropped digit is 5, the preceding digit is raised if odd and left unchanged if even})\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(19.2;\ 7.9;\ 4;\ 4;\ 6.38,\ 6.36\)
Given: \(\text{measured values as stated}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{addition: keep the least number of decimal places; multiplication: keep the least number of significant figures; leading zeros do not count, trailing zeros after a decimal point count}\)
Step 1: \(3.42+15.7+0.128=19.248\to19.2\ (\text{one decimal place, as in }15.7)\)
Step 2: \(2.5\times3.142=7.855\to7.9\ (\text{two significant figures, as in }2.5)\)
Step 3: \(0.03040:\ 3,0,4,0\Rightarrow4;\ 5.000\times10^3\Rightarrow4;\ 6.375\to6.38\ (7\text{ odd}),\ 6.365\to6.36\ (6\text{ even})\)
Worked derivation: \[0.0\underline{3040}:\ \text{zeros before 3 are place holders; the final zero after the decimal point is significant}\]
Check: \[\text{the result cannot be more precise than the least precise measurement}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{significant figures carry the uncertainty of the measurement, which arithmetic cannot reduce}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{unrounded results; counts wrong}\); (C) \(\text{too many digits retained; counts wrong}\); (D) \(\text{too few digits; counts wrong}\).
Key point: \(\text{add: least decimals; multiply: least sig figs; 5-rule: odd up, even same}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the maximum safe speed of a car on a level curve with friction and the friction-free speed on a banked road, and how these speeds scale with the radius of the curve
questions.question: A car takes a level curve of radius \(50\text{ m}\) with \(\mu_s=0.4\) (\(g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}\)). Find the maximum safe speed. If the curve is banked with \(\tan\theta=0.2\), find the speed at which no friction is needed. How does each speed change if the radius is doubled?
options: A) \(\sqrt{200}\approx14.1\text{ m s}^{-1};\ \sqrt{100}=10\text{ m s}^{-1};\ \text{both increase by a factor }\sqrt2,\ \text{since }v\propto\sqrt r\)
B) \(20\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 14.1\text{ m s}^{-1};\ \text{doubles}\)
C) \(200\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 100\text{ m s}^{-1};\ \text{halves}\)
D) \(14.1\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 10\text{ m s}^{-1};\ \text{unchanged}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(14.1\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 10\text{ m s}^{-1};\ \times\sqrt2\)
Given: \(r=50\text{ m},\ \mu_s=0.4,\ \tan\theta=0.2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{level: }\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\le\mu_smg\Rightarrow v_{\max}=\sqrt{\mu_srg};\ \text{banked, no friction: }v_0=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta}\)
Step 1: \(v_{\max}=\sqrt{0.4\times50\times10}=\sqrt{200}=14.1\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(v_0=\sqrt{50\times10\times0.2}=\sqrt{100}=10\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Step 3: \(r\to2r\Rightarrow v\to\sqrt2\,v\)
Worked derivation: \[N\cos\theta=mg,\ N\sin\theta=\frac{mv_0^2}{r}\Rightarrow\tan\theta=\frac{v_0^2}{rg}\]
Check: \[\frac{v_{\max}^2}{r}=\frac{200}{50}=4=\mu_sg\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the centripetal force needed grows as }v^2/r,\ \text{so a wider curve allows a higher speed}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{values wrong; }v\propto\sqrt r\); (C) \(\text{forgot square roots}\); (D) \(\text{speeds depend on }r\).
Key point: \(v_{\max}=\sqrt{\mu rg};\ v_0=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing final velocities and kinetic energy loss for elastic and perfectly inelastic one-dimensional collisions of unequal masses, and the right-angle rule for equal-mass elastic glancing collisions
questions.question: A \(2\text{ kg}\) ball moving at \(6\text{ m s}^{-1}\) hits a \(1\text{ kg}\) ball at rest. Find the final velocities if the collision is (i) perfectly elastic, (ii) perfectly inelastic, and the kinetic energy lost in (ii). What is special when two equal masses collide elastically and obliquely with one initially at rest?
options: B) \((i)\ 4\text{ and }4;\ (ii)\ 2\text{ and }8;\ 12\text{ J}\)
C) \((i)\ 2\text{ and }8\text{ m s}^{-1};\ (ii)\ 4\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 36\text{ J}\)

D) \((i)\ 2\text{ m s}^{-1}\text{ and }8\text{ m s}^{-1};\ (ii)\ 4\text{ m s}^{-1}\text{ together};\ 12\text{ J lost }(36\to24\text{ J});\ \text{the two balls move off at right angles to each other}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\text{elastic: }2\text{ and }8\text{ m s}^{-1};\ \text{inelastic: }4\text{ m s}^{-1},\ 12\text{ J lost};\ \text{equal masses separate at }90^\circ\)
Given: \(m_1=2\text{ kg},\ u_1=6\text{ m s}^{-1};\ m_2=1\text{ kg},\ u_2=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{elastic: }v_1=\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{m_1+m_2}u_1,\ v_2=\dfrac{2m_1}{m_1+m_2}u_1;\ \text{inelastic: }v=\dfrac{m_1u_1}{m_1+m_2}\)
Step 1: \(v_1=\tfrac13\times6=2,\ v_2=\tfrac43\times6=8\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(v=\tfrac{12}{3}=4\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Step 3: \(K_i=\tfrac12(2)(36)=36\text{ J};\ K_f=\tfrac12(3)(16)=24\text{ J};\ \text{loss }12\text{ J}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{equal masses, elastic: }\vec u_1=\vec v_1+\vec v_2,\ u_1^2=v_1^2+v_2^2\Rightarrow\vec v_1\cdot\vec v_2=0\]
Check: \[\text{elastic: }p=2(2)+1(8)=12=2(6);\ K=\tfrac12(2)(4)+\tfrac12(1)(64)=36\ \text{J}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{momentum is conserved in every collision, but kinetic energy only in elastic ones}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{velocities wrong; energy is lost in (ii)}\); (B) \(\text{cases swapped}\); (C) \(\text{loss is }12\text{ J, not }36\text{ J}\).
Key point: \(p\text{ always conserved};\ K\text{ conserved only if elastic}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.sub_topic: Solving a rotational motion problem with constant torque using the rotational analogues of linear equations, and checking the work–energy theorem and power for rotation
questions.question: A flywheel with \(I=2.0\text{ kg m}^2\) starts from rest under a constant torque of \(10\text{ N m}\). After \(4.0\text{ s}\) find its angular velocity, angle turned, kinetic energy, work done by the torque and the power delivered at that instant. Which analogy is correct?
options: A) \(\omega=20\text{ rad s}^{-1};\ \theta=40\text{ rad};\ K=400\text{ J};\ W=\tau\theta=400\text{ J};\ P=\tau\omega=200\text{ W};\ \text{analogues: }m\leftrightarrow I,\ F\leftrightarrow\tau,\ p\leftrightarrow L=I\omega,\ \tfrac12mv^2\leftrightarrow\tfrac12I\omega^2,\ Fv\leftrightarrow\tau\omega\)
B) \(\omega=5\text{ rad s}^{-1};\ \theta=10\text{ rad};\ K=25\text{ J};\ W=100\text{ J}\)
C) \(\omega=80\text{ rad s}^{-1};\ \theta=160\text{ rad};\ K=6400\text{ J}\)
D) \(\omega=20\text{ rad s}^{-1};\ \theta=80\text{ rad};\ K=800\text{ J};\ \text{torque is analogous to mass}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\omega=20\text{ rad s}^{-1},\ \theta=40\text{ rad},\ K=W=400\text{ J},\ P=200\text{ W}\)
Given: \(I=2.0\text{ kg m}^2,\ \tau=10\text{ N m},\ t=4.0\text{ s},\ \omega_0=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\alpha=\dfrac\tau I;\ \omega=\alpha t;\ \theta=\tfrac12\alpha t^2;\ K=\tfrac12I\omega^2;\ P=\tau\omega\)
Step 1: \(\alpha=5\text{ rad s}^{-2}\Rightarrow\omega=20\text{ rad s}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(\theta=\tfrac12(5)(16)=40\text{ rad};\ W=10\times40=400\text{ J}\)
Step 3: \(K=\tfrac12(2)(400)=400\text{ J};\ P=10\times20=200\text{ W}\)
Worked derivation: \[W=\int\tau\,d\theta=\tau\theta=\Delta K=\tfrac12I\omega^2\]
Check: \[W=K=400\ \text{J (work–energy theorem for rotation)}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{rotational equations have the same form as linear ones with }I,\tau,\omega,\theta\text{ replacing }m,F,v,x\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\alpha\text{ used as }\omega\); (C) \(\text{used }\tau I\text{ instead of }\tau/I\); (D) \(\theta=\tfrac12\alpha t^2;\ \tau\leftrightarrow F\).
Key point: \(\tau=I\alpha;\ W=\tau\theta;\ P=\tau\omega\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating orbital speed and kinetic, potential and total energies of a satellite at twice the Earth's radius, and the energy needed to place it in orbit from the surface by energy conservation
questions.question: A \(200\text{ kg}\) satellite orbits at radius \(2R_E\) (\(R_E=6.4\times10^6\text{ m},\ g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}\)). Find its orbital speed, kinetic, potential and total energies, and the minimum energy needed to put it in this orbit from the surface (ignoring Earth's rotation).
options: C) \(5.66\text{ km s}^{-1};\ K=3.2\times10^9\text{ J};\ U=-6.4\times10^9\text{ J};\ E=-3.2\times10^9\text{ J};\ \Delta E=\tfrac34mgR_E=9.6\times10^9\text{ J}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(v_0\approx5.66\text{ km s}^{-1};\ K=3.2\times10^9,\ U=-6.4\times10^9,\ E=-3.2\times10^9\text{ J};\ 9.6\times10^9\text{ J}\)
Given: \(m=200\text{ kg},\ r=2R_E;\ GM=gR_E^2\)
Formula/Principle: \(v_0=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}};\ K=\dfrac{GMm}{2r},\ U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r},\ E=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\)
Step 1: \(v_0=\sqrt{\dfrac{gR_E}{2}}=\sqrt{3.2\times10^7}=5.66\times10^3\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(K=\dfrac{mgR_E}{4}=\dfrac{200\times10\times6.4\times10^6}{4}=3.2\times10^9\text{ J};\ U=-2K;\ E=-K\)
Step 3: \(\Delta E=E_{\text{orbit}}-E_{\text{surface}}=-\dfrac{mgR_E}{4}-(-mgR_E)=\tfrac34mgR_E=9.6\times10^9\text{ J}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{mv_0^2}{r}=\frac{GMm}{r^2}\Rightarrow\tfrac12mv_0^2=\frac{GMm}{2r}=-\tfrac12U\]
Check: \[K+U=3.2\times10^9-6.4\times10^9=-3.2\times10^9\ \text{J}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a bound orbit has negative total energy equal to minus its kinetic energy}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{values for a surface orbit; total energy is not zero}\); (B) \(\text{escape speed is not orbital speed}\); (D) \(K\text{ and }U\text{ mismatched; }E<0\).
Key point: \(E=-K=\tfrac12U=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Explaining capillary rise and depression from contact angle, calculating the rise of water in a glass tube, and the excess pressure inside drops and soap bubbles
questions.question: Water (\(S=0.073\text{ N m}^{-1}\), contact angle \(\approx0^\circ\)) rises in a glass capillary of radius \(0.50\text{ mm}\) (\(g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}\)). Which statement is correct?
options: A) Water rises \(h=\dfrac{2S\cos\theta}{\rho gr}=\dfrac{2\times0.073}{1000\times10\times5\times10^{-4}}\approx2.9\text{ cm}\); mercury, with contact angle about \(140^\circ\) (obtuse), is depressed in the same tube; the excess pressure inside a liquid drop is \(2S/R\) and inside a soap bubble \(4S/R\) because a bubble has two surfaces; detergents lower surface tension so water wets greasy fabric better
B) Water is depressed in glass because its contact angle is obtuse; a soap bubble has excess pressure \(2S/R\)
C) Capillary rise is greater in a wider tube
D) Surface tension increases when detergent is added
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(h\approx2.9\text{ cm};\ \text{mercury depressed};\ \text{drop }2S/R,\ \text{bubble }4S/R;\ \text{detergents lower }S\)
Given: \(S=0.073\text{ N m}^{-1},\ \theta=0,\ r=5\times10^{-4}\text{ m},\ \rho=1000\text{ kg m}^{-3}\)
Formula/Principle: \(h=\dfrac{2S\cos\theta}{\rho gr};\ \Delta p_{\text{drop}}=\dfrac{2S}{R},\ \Delta p_{\text{bubble}}=\dfrac{4S}{R}\)
Step 1: \(2S\cos\theta=0.146\)
Step 2: \(\rho gr=1000\times10\times5\times10^{-4}=5\)
Step 3: \(h=0.146/5=0.0292\text{ m}=2.9\text{ cm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{upward surface force }2\pi rS\cos\theta=\text{weight of column }\pi r^2h\rho g\Rightarrow h=\frac{2S\cos\theta}{\rho gr}\]
Check: \[\theta>90^\circ\Rightarrow\cos\theta<0\Rightarrow h<0\ (\text{depression, as for mercury})\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the liquid rises until the vertical pull of surface tension balances the weight of the raised column}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{water wets glass (acute angle); bubble has }4S/R\); (C) \(h\propto1/r\); (D) \(\text{detergents reduce }S\).
Key point: \(h=2S\cos\theta/\rho gr;\ \text{drop }2S/R,\ \text{bubble }4S/R\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using Wien's displacement law to estimate the Sun's surface temperature, the T^4 scaling of radiated power, and Newton's law of cooling to find a cooling constant and read the cooling graph
questions.question: The Sun's spectrum peaks near \(500\text{ nm}\) (\(b=2.9\times10^{-3}\text{ m K}\)). Estimate its surface temperature. By what factor does a body's radiated power change if its absolute temperature doubles? A liquid cools from \(80^\circ\text{C}\) to \(60^\circ\text{C}\) in 5 min in a room at \(20^\circ\text{C}\); using the average-temperature form of Newton's law, find the cooling constant. Which graph of \(\ln(T-T_s)\) against \(t\) is expected?
options: A) \(1450\text{ K};\ 2;\ 0.4\text{ min}^{-1};\ \text{parabola}\)
B) \(5800\text{ K};\ 4;\ 0.08\text{ min}^{-1};\ \text{rising straight line}\)
C) \(\approx5800\text{ K};\ 16\ (P\propto T^4);\ k=\dfrac{(80-60)/5}{70-20}=0.08\text{ min}^{-1};\ \text{a straight line with negative slope }-k\)
D) \(5800\text{ K};\ 16;\ 0.08\text{ min}^{-1};\ \text{horizontal line}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\approx5800\text{ K};\ 16\times;\ k=0.08\text{ min}^{-1};\ \text{straight line of slope }-k\)
Given: \(\lambda_m=5.0\times10^{-7}\text{ m};\ 80\to60^\circ\text{C in }5\text{ min},\ T_s=20^\circ\text{C}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\lambda_mT=b;\ P=\sigma AeT^4;\ \dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-T_s)\)
Step 1: \(T=\dfrac{2.9\times10^{-3}}{5.0\times10^{-7}}=5800\text{ K}\)
Step 2: \(T\to2T\Rightarrow P\to2^4P=16P\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{20}{5}=k(70-20)\Rightarrow k=\dfrac{4}{50}=0.08\text{ min}^{-1}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{dT}{T-T_s}=-k\,dt\Rightarrow\ln(T-T_s)=-kt+C\]
Check: \[\text{rate at average temperature }70^\circ\text{C}:\ 0.08\times50=4\ ^\circ\text{C min}^{-1}=20/5\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths, radiate far more strongly, and cool exponentially towards room temperature}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{temperature and scalings wrong}\); (B) \(P\propto T^4;\ \text{slope negative}\); (D) \(\text{the graph slopes downward}\).
Key point: \(\lambda_mT=b;\ P\propto T^4;\ \ln(T-T_s)\text{ linear in }t\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Applying the first law to isobaric, isochoric, isothermal and adiabatic processes of a monatomic ideal gas and comparing isothermal and adiabatic curves on a P–V graph
questions.question: A monatomic ideal gas expands at constant pressure \(2.0\times10^5\text{ Pa}\) from \(1.0\text{ L}\) to \(3.0\text{ L}\). Find the work done, \(\Delta U\) and the heat supplied. Which statement about P–V graphs from a common initial state is correct?
options: A) \(W=600\text{ J};\ \Delta U=400\text{ J};\ Q=1000\text{ J};\ \text{isothermal curve is steeper}\)
B) \(W=400\text{ J};\ \Delta U=0;\ Q=400\text{ J};\ \text{both curves have the same slope}\)

C) \(W=400\text{ J};\ \Delta U=600\text{ J};\ Q=1000\text{ J};\ \text{the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal one (slope }-\gamma P/V\text{ against }-P/V),\ \text{so an adiabatic expansion does less work; in an isochoric process }W=0\text{ and }Q=\Delta U,\ \text{and in an isothermal process }\Delta U=0\text{ and }Q=W\)
D) \(W=400\text{ J};\ \Delta U=1000\text{ J};\ Q=600\text{ J};\ \text{adiabatic process has }W=0\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(W=400\text{ J},\ \Delta U=600\text{ J},\ Q=1000\text{ J};\ \text{adiabatic steeper}\)
Given: \(P=2.0\times10^5\text{ Pa},\ \Delta V=2.0\times10^{-3}\text{ m}^3;\ C_v=\tfrac32R\)
Formula/Principle: \(W=P\Delta V;\ \Delta U=nC_v\Delta T=\tfrac32P\Delta V;\ Q=\Delta U+W\)
Step 1: \(W=2.0\times10^5\times2.0\times10^{-3}=400\text{ J}\)
Step 2: \(\Delta U=\tfrac32\times400=600\text{ J}\)
Step 3: \(Q=600+400=1000\text{ J}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{isothermal: }PV=c\Rightarrow\frac{dP}{dV}=-\frac PV;\quad\text{adiabatic: }PV^\gamma=c\Rightarrow\frac{dP}{dV}=-\gamma\frac PV\]
Check: \[Q=nC_p\Delta T=\tfrac52P\Delta V=\tfrac52\times400=1000\ \text{J}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{in an adiabatic expansion the gas cools, so its pressure falls faster than at constant temperature}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(W\text{ and }\Delta U\text{ swapped; adiabatic is steeper}\); (B) \(\Delta U\ne0\text{ since }T\text{ rises}\); (D) \(\text{signs mixed; adiabatic means }Q=0\).
Key point: \(Q=\Delta U+W;\ \text{adiabatic slope}=\gamma\times\text{isothermal slope}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using the law of equipartition of energy to find molar specific heats and γ for monatomic and diatomic gases and a mixture, and reading how Cv of a diatomic gas rises with temperature
questions.question: Using equipartition, give \(C_v\) and \(\gamma\) for helium and for rigid diatomic oxygen, and \(C_v,\ C_p,\ \gamma\) for a mixture of 1 mol He and 1 mol O₂. What happens to \(C_v\) of a diatomic gas at high temperature, and what is \(C_v\) of a solid (per mole)?
options: A) \(\text{He: }\tfrac52R,\ \tfrac75;\ \text{O}_2:\ \tfrac32R,\ \tfrac53;\ \text{mixture }C_v=4R\)
B) \(\text{He: }\tfrac32R,\ \tfrac53;\ \text{O}_2:\ \tfrac52R,\ \tfrac75;\ \text{mixture }C_v=4R,\ C_p=5R,\ \gamma=1.25\)
C) \(\text{He: }3R,\ \tfrac43;\ \text{O}_2:\ 3R;\ \text{mixture }\gamma=1.67\)

D) \(\text{He: }\tfrac32R,\ \gamma=\tfrac53;\ \text{O}_2:\ \tfrac52R,\ \gamma=\tfrac75;\ \text{mixture }C_v=2R,\ C_p=3R,\ \gamma=1.5;\ \text{at high temperature vibrational modes add }R\text{, giving }C_v=\tfrac72R;\ \text{solids have }C_v\approx3R\ (\text{Dulong–Petit})\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\text{He }\tfrac32R,\ \tfrac53;\ \text{O}_2\ \tfrac52R,\ \tfrac75;\ \text{mixture }2R,\ 3R,\ 1.5;\ \text{diatomic }\to\tfrac72R;\ \text{solid }3R\)
Given: \(\text{He: 3 translational dof};\ \text{O}_2:\ 3\text{ translational}+2\text{ rotational}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{each quadratic term gets }\tfrac12k_BT;\ C_v=\tfrac f2R,\ C_p=C_v+R;\ \text{mixture }C_v=\dfrac{\sum n_iC_{v,i}}{\sum n_i}\)
Step 1: \(\text{He: }f=3\Rightarrow C_v=\tfrac32R,\ \gamma=\tfrac{5/2}{3/2}=\tfrac53\)
Step 2: \(\text{O}_2:\ f=5\Rightarrow C_v=\tfrac52R,\ \gamma=\tfrac75\)
Step 3: \(\text{mixture }C_v=\dfrac{\frac32R+\frac52R}{2}=2R,\ C_p=3R,\ \gamma=1.5\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{vibration adds kinetic and potential terms: }2\times\tfrac12k_BT\Rightarrow C_v=\tfrac52R+R=\tfrac72R\]
Check: \[\text{solid: 3 oscillators per atom}\times(\tfrac12+\tfrac12)k_BT\times N_A=3RT\Rightarrow C_v=3R\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each active degree of freedom stores the same average energy, so more modes mean a higher specific heat}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{values swapped; mixture miscomputed}\); (B) \(\text{mixture values not averaged per mole}\); (C) \(\text{wrong degrees of freedom}\).
Key point: \(C_v=\tfrac f2R;\ \gamma=1+\tfrac2f\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Reading amplitude, period and initial phase of an oscillator from sensor data, writing its equation, and finding maximum velocity, maximum acceleration and velocity at a given displacement with phase relations
questions.question: A motion sensor records an oscillator with amplitude \(4.0\text{ cm}\) and period \(0.50\text{ s}\); at \(t=0\) it is at \(x=+2.0\text{ cm}\) moving towards \(+x\). Write \(x(t)\) and find the maximum speed, maximum acceleration and speed at \(x=2.0\text{ cm}\). How are velocity and acceleration related in phase to displacement?
options: B) \(x=4\cos(4\pi t+\tfrac\pi6);\ 50\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ 632\text{ cm s}^{-2};\ 50\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ \text{all in phase}\)
C) \(x=2\sin(4\pi t);\ 25\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ 316\text{ cm s}^{-2};\ 0;\ \text{velocity lags by }\pi\)

D) \(x=4\sin\!\left(4\pi t+\tfrac\pi6\right)\text{ cm};\ v_{\max}=A\omega\approx50.3\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ a_{\max}=A\omega^2\approx632\text{ cm s}^{-2};\ v=\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2}\approx43.5\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ \text{velocity leads displacement by }\tfrac\pi2,\ \text{acceleration leads by }\pi\ (a=-\omega^2x)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(x=4\sin(4\pi t+\tfrac\pi6);\ 50.3\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ 632\text{ cm s}^{-2};\ 43.5\text{ cm s}^{-1}\)
Given: \(A=4.0\text{ cm},\ T=0.50\text{ s},\ x(0)=2.0\text{ cm},\ v(0)>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi);\ \omega=\tfrac{2\pi}T;\ v=\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2};\ a=-\omega^2x\)
Step 1: \(\omega=4\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1};\ \sin\phi=\tfrac12,\ \cos\phi>0\Rightarrow\phi=\tfrac\pi6\)
Step 2: \(v_{\max}=4\times4\pi=50.3\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ a_{\max}=4\times16\pi^2=632\text{ cm s}^{-2}\)
Step 3: \(v=4\pi\sqrt{16-4}=4\pi\times3.46=43.5\text{ cm s}^{-1}\)
Worked derivation: \[v=\frac{dx}{dt}=A\omega\cos(\omega t+\phi)=A\omega\sin\left(\omega t+\phi+\tfrac\pi2\right),\quad a=-A\omega^2\sin(\omega t+\phi)\]
Check: \[v(0)=A\omega\cos\tfrac\pi6=50.3\times0.866=43.5\ \text{cm s}^{-1}>0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the initial position and direction of motion fix the phase constant uniquely}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\omega=2\pi/T=4\pi\); (B) \(\text{cosine with }\pi/6\text{ gives }x(0)=3.46\text{ cm; phases differ}\); (C) \(\text{amplitude and phase wrong}\).
Key point: \(\phi\text{ from }x(0)\text{ and sign of }v(0);\ v\text{ leads }x\text{ by }\pi/2,\ a\text{ by }\pi\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding an unknown frequency from beats with a standard tuning fork and the change in beat rate on loading with wax, and calculating beat frequency and period of two close tones
questions.question: A tuning fork of \(256\text{ Hz}\) sounded with an unknown fork gives 4 beats per second. When the unknown fork is loaded with a little wax, the beats fall to 2 per second. Find the unknown frequency. Two tones of 400 Hz and 404 Hz are sounded together; find the beat frequency and beat period.
options: A) \(252\text{ Hz};\ 2\text{ Hz};\ 0.5\text{ s}\)
B) \(260\text{ Hz (loading lowers its frequency, bringing it closer to 256 Hz)};\ 4\text{ Hz};\ 0.25\text{ s}\)
D) \(252\text{ Hz};\ 4\text{ Hz};\ 4\text{ s}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(260\text{ Hz};\ 4\text{ Hz};\ 0.25\text{ s}\)
Given: \(f_0=256\text{ Hz},\ \text{beats }4\to2\text{ after loading};\ 400,\ 404\text{ Hz}\)
Formula/Principle: \(f_{\text{beat}}=|f_1-f_2|;\ \text{loading a fork lowers its frequency}\)
Step 1: \(f=256\pm4=252\text{ or }260\text{ Hz}\)
Step 2: \(\text{loading lowers }f;\ \text{beats decrease}\Rightarrow f\text{ moved towards }256\Rightarrow f=260\text{ Hz (becomes 258 Hz)}\)
Step 3: \(f_{\text{beat}}=404-400=4\text{ Hz};\ T_b=\tfrac14=0.25\text{ s}\)
Worked derivation: \[y=2a\cos\left(2\pi\frac{f_1-f_2}{2}t\right)\sin\left(2\pi\frac{f_1+f_2}{2}t\right)\Rightarrow\text{loudness maxima }|f_1-f_2|\text{ times per second}\]
Check: \[\text{if }f\text{ were }252\text{ Hz, loading would lower it further and beats would rise above 4}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the direction in which the beat rate changes tells which side of the standard the unknown lies}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{252 Hz would give more beats after loading}\); (C) \(\text{beat frequency is the difference}\); (D) \(\text{frequency and period wrong}\).
Key point: \(f_{\text{beat}}=|f_1-f_2|;\ \text{wax lowers frequency}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the electric fields of an infinite line charge, an infinite plane sheet and a uniformly charged spherical shell derived from Gauss's law, including their distance dependence
questions.question: Using Gauss's law, which comparison of fields is correct? (A long wire has \(\lambda=2.0\times10^{-7}\text{ C m}^{-1}\); \(k=9\times10^9\text{ N m}^2\text{ C}^{-2}\).)
options: A) The field of a line charge is independent of distance; a sheet's field falls as \(1/r^2\); inside a charged shell the field is \(kq/R^2\)

B) Line charge: \(E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}=\dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}\propto\dfrac1r\), so at \(0.10\text{ m}\) from the wire \(E=3.6\times10^4\text{ N C}^{-1}\); infinite sheet: \(E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\), independent of distance; two parallel sheets with \(\pm\sigma\) give \(\sigma/\varepsilon_0\) between them and zero outside; uniformly charged shell: \(E=\dfrac{kq}{r^2}\) outside (as if all charge were at the centre) and \(E=0\) inside
C) All three fields fall off as \(1/r^2\)
D) The field inside a uniformly charged shell is largest at its centre
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\text{line }\propto1/r\ (3.6\times10^4\text{ N C}^{-1});\ \text{sheet constant};\ \text{shell }kq/r^2\text{ outside, }0\text{ inside}\)
Given: \(\lambda=2.0\times10^{-7}\text{ C m}^{-1},\ r=0.10\text{ m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\text{ with cylindrical, pill-box and spherical Gaussian surfaces}\)
Step 1: \(\text{cylinder: }E(2\pi rl)=\dfrac{\lambda l}{\varepsilon_0}\Rightarrow E=\dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}=\dfrac{2\times9\times10^9\times2\times10^{-7}}{0.10}=3.6\times10^4\text{ N C}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(\text{pill-box: }2EA=\dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}\Rightarrow E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\)
Step 3: \(\text{sphere: }E(4\pi r^2)=\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\ (r>R);\ q_{\text{enc}}=0\ (r<R)\Rightarrow E=0\)
Worked derivation: \[E_{\text{between}}=\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}+\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0},\quad E_{\text{outside}}=\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}-\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}=0\]
Check: \[\text{line field drops to half when }r\text{ doubles: }1.8\times10^4\ \text{N C}^{-1}\text{ at }0.20\ \text{m}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the symmetry of each charge distribution decides how the Gaussian area grows with distance}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{dependences swapped; shell interior is field-free}\); (C) \(\text{only the shell exterior is }1/r^2\); (D) \(E=0\text{ everywhere inside}\).
Key point: \(\text{line }1/r;\ \text{sheet constant};\ \text{shell }1/r^2\text{ outside, }0\text{ inside}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the change in capacitance, charge, voltage and stored energy when a dielectric slab fills a capacitor with the battery connected and disconnected, and reading energy as area under the Q–V graph
questions.question: A \(10\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor is charged to \(100\text{ V}\). A dielectric of \(K=4\) then fills it (i) with the battery still connected, (ii) after the battery is disconnected. Find the initial energy and the charge, voltage and energy in each case. What does the area under a charge–voltage graph represent?
options: A) \(0.05\text{ J};\ (i)\ 1\text{ mC},\ 100\text{ V},\ 0.05\text{ J};\ (ii)\ 4\text{ mC},\ 400\text{ V},\ 0.8\text{ J};\ \text{charge}\)
B) \(0.5\text{ J};\ (i)\ 4\text{ mC},\ 25\text{ V};\ (ii)\ 1\text{ mC},\ 100\text{ V};\ \text{capacitance}\)

C) \(0.05\text{ J};\ (i)\ 4\text{ mC},\ 100\text{ V},\ 0.2\text{ J};\ (ii)\ 1\text{ mC},\ 25\text{ V},\ 0.0125\text{ J};\ \text{the stored energy }\tfrac12QV,\ \text{since the }Q\text{–}V\text{ graph is a straight line of slope }C\)
D) \(0.05\text{ J};\ (i)\ 4\text{ mC},\ 100\text{ V},\ 0.0125\text{ J};\ (ii)\ 1\text{ mC},\ 25\text{ V},\ 0.2\text{ J};\ \text{power}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(U_0=0.05\text{ J};\ \text{(i) }4\text{ mC},\ 100\text{ V},\ 0.2\text{ J};\ \text{(ii) }1\text{ mC},\ 25\text{ V},\ 0.0125\text{ J};\ \text{area}=\text{energy}\)
Given: \(C_0=10\ \mu\text{F},\ V_0=100\text{ V},\ K=4\)
Formula/Principle: \(C=KC_0;\ Q=CV;\ U=\tfrac12CV^2=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}\)
Step 1: \(U_0=\tfrac12\times10^{-5}\times10^4=0.05\text{ J};\ Q_0=1\text{ mC}\)
Step 2: \(\text{(i) }V\text{ fixed}:\ C=40\ \mu\text{F},\ Q=4\text{ mC},\ U=\tfrac12\times4\times10^{-5}\times10^4=0.2\text{ J}\)
Step 3: \(\text{(ii) }Q\text{ fixed}:\ V=\tfrac{100}{4}=25\text{ V},\ U=\dfrac{(10^{-3})^2}{2\times4\times10^{-5}}=0.0125\text{ J}\)
Worked derivation: \[U=\int_0^QV\,dq=\int_0^Q\frac qC\,dq=\frac{Q^2}{2C}=\tfrac12QV\]
Check: \[\text{(ii) }U=U_0/K=0.05/4=0.0125\ \text{J};\ \text{(i) }U=KU_0=0.2\ \text{J}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a connected battery holds }V\text{ fixed and supplies extra charge; an isolated capacitor keeps }Q\text{ fixed}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{cases reversed and wrong}\); (B) \(\text{energy and cases wrong}\); (D) \(\text{energies swapped}\).
Key point: \(\text{battery on: }V\text{ fixed, }U\times K;\ \text{off: }Q\text{ fixed, }U/K\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Testing balance of a Wheatstone bridge, finding an unknown resistance from a metre bridge null point, and stating the physical basis of Kirchhoff's junction and loop rules
questions.question: In a Wheatstone bridge \(P=10\ \Omega,\ Q=20\ \Omega,\ R=15\ \Omega,\ S=30\ \Omega\). Is it balanced? In a metre bridge with \(2.0\ \Omega\) in the left gap, the null point is at \(40.0\text{ cm}\) from the left end; find the resistance in the right gap. On what conservation laws are Kirchhoff's rules based?
options: A) \(\text{balanced (}P/Q=R/S=\tfrac12),\ \text{so no current flows through the galvanometer};\ S=2.0\times\tfrac{60}{40}=3.0\ \Omega;\ \text{junction rule: conservation of charge; loop rule: conservation of energy}\)
B) \(\text{not balanced};\ 1.33\ \Omega;\ \text{junction rule: energy; loop rule: charge}\)
C) \(\text{balanced};\ 0.8\ \Omega;\ \text{both from Ohm's law}\)
D) \(\text{not balanced};\ 3.0\ \Omega;\ \text{loop rule: conservation of momentum}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\text{balanced};\ S=3.0\ \Omega;\ \text{charge and energy conservation}\)
Given: \(P,Q,R,S;\ R_{\text{left}}=2.0\ \Omega,\ l=40.0\text{ cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{balance: }\dfrac PQ=\dfrac RS;\ \text{metre bridge: }\dfrac{R}{S}=\dfrac{l}{100-l}\)
Step 1: \(\tfrac{10}{20}=\tfrac{15}{30}=\tfrac12\Rightarrow\text{balanced}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{2.0}{S}=\dfrac{40}{60}\Rightarrow S=3.0\ \Omega\)
Step 3: \(\sum I_{\text{in}}=\sum I_{\text{out}}\ (\text{charge});\ \sum\Delta V=0\text{ round a loop (energy)}\)
Worked derivation: \[I_g=0\Rightarrow V_B=V_D\Rightarrow I_1P=I_2R,\ I_1Q=I_2S\Rightarrow\frac PQ=\frac RS\]
Check: \[\text{wire resistance}\propto\text{length}:\ \frac{40}{60}=\frac{2.0}{3.0}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at balance the galvanometer ends are at the same potential, so the ratio arms match}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{ratio inverted; rules swapped}\); (C) \(\text{metre-bridge ratio wrong}\); (D) \(\text{bridge is balanced; loop rule is energy}\).
Key point: \(P/Q=R/S;\ \text{junction}=\text{charge},\ \text{loop}=\text{energy}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using the Biot–Savart law to find the magnetic field at the centre and on the axis of a circular coil and near a long straight wire
questions.question: A circular coil of 100 turns and radius \(0.10\text{ m}\) carries \(1.0\text{ A}\) (\(\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\)). Find the field at its centre and on its axis at a distance equal to its radius. Find also the field \(5.0\text{ cm}\) from a long straight wire carrying \(10\text{ A}\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(B_0=6.28\times10^{-4}\text{ T};\ B_{\text{axis}}=2.22\times10^{-4}\text{ T};\ 4.0\times10^{-5}\text{ T}\)
Given: \(N=100,\ R=0.10\text{ m},\ I=1.0\text{ A};\ x=R;\ \text{wire }I=10\text{ A},\ r=0.050\text{ m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(dB=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2};\ B_{\text{axis}}=\dfrac{\mu_0NIR^2}{2(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}};\ B_{\text{wire}}=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}\)
Step 1: \(B_0=\dfrac{\mu_0NI}{2R}=\dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times100}{0.20}=6.28\times10^{-4}\text{ T}\)
Step 2: \(x=R:\ B=\dfrac{\mu_0NIR^2}{2(2R^2)^{3/2}}=\dfrac{B_0}{2\sqrt2}=2.22\times10^{-4}\text{ T}\)
Step 3: \(B_{\text{wire}}=\dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times10}{2\pi\times0.05}=4.0\times10^{-5}\text{ T}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{centre: every element is perpendicular to }\vec r\text{ at distance }R:\ B=N\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi R^2}(2\pi R)=\frac{\mu_0NI}{2R}\]
Check: \[(R^2+R^2)^{3/2}=2\sqrt2R^3\Rightarrow B_{\text{axis}}/B_0=1/(2\sqrt2)=0.354\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{on the axis only the axial components of the elemental fields add, and they weaken with distance}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{axial factor and wire field halved}\); (C) \(\text{factor 2 error at the centre}\); (D) \(\text{forgot }N\text{ and the }10^2\text{ scale}\).
Key point: \(B_0=\mu_0NI/2R;\ B_{\text{axis}}(x=R)=B_0/2\sqrt2;\ B_{\text{wire}}=\mu_0I/2\pi r\)
